stem: A trading firm must survive the loss of an entire data center with no data loss for its order database, keep synchronous-replication latency in the low milliseconds, and also tolerate a full Regional outage with a recovery time of under an hour. Which architecture meets all three goals?

choices.text: Synchronous replication across two Regions, since Regions are designed for low-latency interconnection
Synchronous replication across AZs, plus async replication to a second Region
Multiple instances in one AZ on separate racks, plus nightly snapshots copied to a second Region
Asynchronous replication across AZs, plus synchronous replication to a second Region for zero data loss

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Availability Zones in a Region are physically separate (independent power, cooling, and networking) but connected with low-latency private links, which makes synchronous replication practical, so losing one data center or AZ loses no data. Regions are far apart, so replication between them is normally asynchronous. That meets an RTO under an hour for a Regional failure, accepting a small RPO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous across Regions: inter-Region distance adds latency far above low milliseconds, which would slow every write.
• Racks in one AZ: an AZ-level event takes all of them down, and nightly snapshots give a large RPO.
• Async within the Region, sync across Regions: backwards. It risks data loss for an AZ failure and adds high latency for the cross-Region path.

Key takeaway: AZs are for synchronous, low-latency high availability. Regions are for disaster recovery, usually with asynchronous replication.

stem: A company has VPC-A peered with VPC-B, and VPC-B peered with VPC-C. Instances in VPC-A cannot reach instances in VPC-C despite correct route table entries pointing to the respective peering connections. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The security groups in VPC-C block inbound traffic from VPC-A's CIDR range
VPC-A and VPC-C have overlapping CIDR blocks, so routes to VPC-C cannot be added
Peering is not transitive; use a Transit Gateway or a direct VPC-A to VPC-C peering
The peering connections belong to different AWS Organizations, which blocks forwarding between them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC peering is non-transitive: A can't reach C through B, even with routes. A direct A-C peering or a Transit Gateway (hub-and-spoke routing) is required.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups in C: the traffic never arrives, since peering doesn't forward.
• Overlapping CIDRs: not the stated problem; routes were correct.
• Different Organizations: peering works across accounts and organizations.

Key takeaway: peering is one-to-one; for transitive routing, use Transit Gateway.

stem: A financial services firm requires 99.99% availability for its hybrid connection between on-premises data centers and AWS, with automatic failover and no single point of failure. Which architecture best meets this requirement while balancing cost?

choices.text: One Direct Connect connection at one location with a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as backup
Two Direct Connect connections at the same Direct Connect location, on separate customer routers
Two DX connections at two different DX locations, each reaching AWS through a DX gateway, plus a Site-to-Site VPN as backup
Site-to-Site VPN only, using both tunnels of two VPN connections to separate customer gateways

explanation:
Why this is correct:
99.99% requires no single point of failure at the location level: two connections at two different Direct Connect locations, each with its own device, give automatic BGP failover if a location fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One DX + VPN: VPN backup has variable performance and falls short of the 99.99% design.
• Two connections at one location: a location failure takes both down.
• VPN only: internet-dependent and not suitable for this SLA.

Key takeaway: high resiliency = separate DX locations.

stem: An enterprise has 40 VPCs across multiple accounts that all need to communicate with each other and with an on-premises network via a shared Direct Connect connection. Which approach minimizes operational complexity as the number of VPCs grows?

choices.text: Full-mesh VPC peering between all 40 VPCs, with a virtual private gateway on each VPC for on-premises access
Attach all VPCs to one Transit Gateway connected to DX through a DX gateway
Site-to-Site VPN connections between every pair of VPCs and from each VPC to the data center
Consolidate all workloads into a single large VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke routing for all 40 VPCs, and a Direct Connect gateway with a transit VIF connects that hub to on-premises over the shared DX link.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full mesh peering: 780 connections, and peering can't share DX transitively.
• VPN between every pair: unmanageable.
• One giant VPC: loses account and blast-radius separation.

Key takeaway: many VPCs + on-prem → TGW + DX gateway.

stem: A company runs Active Directory on-premises and needs EC2 instances in a VPC to resolve on-premises hostnames, while on-premises servers must also resolve records in a private hosted zone associated with the VPC. Which solution satisfies both requirements?

choices.text: Resolver inbound endpoints for on-prem lookups and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for on-prem names
A single Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the on-premises Active Directory domain
EC2-based DNS forwarders in the VPC that replace the Route 53 Resolver for all queries
A public hosted zone for the VPC records, with on-premises DNS servers pointed at it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS forward queries into the VPC (for private zones), and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send VPC queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: covers one direction.
• EC2 forwarders replacing Resolver: extra servers to run, and unnecessary.
• Public hosted zone: exposes internal names.

Key takeaway: inbound = on-prem → AWS; outbound = AWS → on-prem.

stem: A team needs private connectivity from a VPC to Amazon S3 without traversing the internet, and separately needs private connectivity to a third-party SaaS API hosted in another VPC. Which combination of VPC endpoints is appropriate?

choices.text: Use gateway endpoints for both S3 and the SaaS API
Use interface endpoints for both S3 and the SaaS API
Use a gateway endpoint for S3 and an interface endpoint (powered by PrivateLink) for the SaaS API
Use an interface endpoint (powered by PrivateLink) for S3 and a gateway endpoint for the SaaS API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 supports gateway endpoints (route table entries, no cost). Third-party SaaS APIs are reached privately through PrivateLink interface endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway for SaaS: gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• Interface for both: works for S3 but costs more; the key point is SaaS needs PrivateLink.
• Reversed: SaaS can't use gateway endpoints.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB → gateway endpoints; everything else → interface endpoints.

stem: A company is designing IP addressing for a new landing zone that will eventually host 200 VPCs across development, staging, and production accounts, and must peer with an on-premises network using 10.0.0.0/8. What is the best practice to avoid future addressing conflicts?

choices.text: Use VPC IPAM to plan and allocate non-overlapping CIDRs across all accounts
Let each account team pick CIDR blocks independently, since IAM policies prevent overlapping ranges
Give every VPC the same /16 CIDR block
Use public IP ranges for all VPCs so addresses are globally unique across the organization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC IPAM plans, allocates, and tracks non-overlapping CIDRs across accounts and Regions from managed pools, preventing conflicts as 200 VPCs are created.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Teams choose independently: overlaps will block future connectivity; IAM doesn't prevent overlap.
• Same /16 everywhere: can't interconnect.
• Public IP ranges: waste scarce addresses and don't fit private networks.

Key takeaway: org-wide IP planning → VPC IPAM.

stem: A healthcare company must guarantee that a Direct Connect failure at any single point (device, connection, or location) does not disrupt connectivity, per AWS's highest resiliency model. Which configuration satisfies this?

choices.text: Four dedicated connections, two at each of two DX locations (maximum resiliency model)
Two dedicated connections at the same location terminating on the same AWS device
One dedicated connection with a hosted connection from a partner at the same location as backup
One dedicated connection paired with a Site-to-Site VPN that terminates in the same location

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maximum resiliency uses separate connections on separate devices at two locations (four connections), surviving a device, connection, or location failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two connections on the same device: device or location failure breaks both.
• Dedicated + hosted at one location: location failure breaks both.
• DX + VPN in the same location's path: not the maximum resiliency model.

Key takeaway: survive any single failure → maximum resiliency (2 locations × 2 devices).

stem: A network team wants centralized, fine-grained control so that a shared services VPC can reach all spoke VPCs, but spoke VPCs cannot communicate directly with each other, all through a single Transit Gateway. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: Attach all VPCs to one TGW route table with default association and propagation enabled for every attachment
Separate TGW route tables: spokes see only shared services; shared services sees all spokes
Use VPC peering between the shared services VPC and each spoke instead of the Transit Gateway
Apply network ACLs on each spoke VPC that deny traffic from the other spoke VPC CIDR ranges

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate TGW route tables: spoke attachments associate with a table that only has routes to shared services, and the shared services table has routes to all spokes. Spokes can't reach each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One table with propagation: every spoke can reach every other spoke.
• Peering: loses central control and doesn't scale.
• NACLs per spoke: brittle and hard to manage.

Key takeaway: segment with TGW route table association and propagation.

stem: Application teams report intermittent connectivity failures between an EC2 instance and an RDS database in the same VPC, but only during specific time windows. Which AWS capability should the architect enable to capture detailed IP-level traffic data for root-cause analysis?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray tracing on the application to capture database call failures
Amazon Inspector network reachability analysis between the two resources
AWS Config configuration history of the security groups involved
VPC Flow Logs on the relevant ENIs, showing which flows were accepted and which were rejected

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Flow Logs on the ENIs record accepted and rejected flows with timestamps, showing whether traffic was blocked during the failure windows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: application traces, not network accept/reject decisions.
• Inspector reachability: static analysis, not what happened at specific times.
• Config history: shows rule changes but not traffic outcomes.

Key takeaway: what actually happened to traffic → Flow Logs.

stem: A SaaS provider wants to expose an internal API running on EC2 instances in its VPC to hundreds of customer VPCs across different AWS accounts, without allowing customers to see or interact with any other resources in the provider's VPC. What should the architect use?

choices.text: VPC peering with each customer VPC and security groups that allow only the API port
Transit Gateway peering shared to every customer account through AWS RAM
A PrivateLink endpoint service backed by an NLB, with each customer creating an interface endpoint
A public Application Load Balancer with per-customer IP allow lists in WAF

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB exposes only the API. Customers create interface endpoints in their VPCs, with no CIDR coordination or full network access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: exposes whole networks and needs non-overlapping CIDRs.
• TGW shared to customers: gives broad network connectivity.
• Public ALB with WAF allow lists: internet exposure.

Key takeaway: expose one service to many VPCs → PrivateLink.

stem: Security wants to block DNS resolution of malicious and newly registered domains from 300 VPCs across 60 accounts, using AWS-managed threat lists, with logs of blocked queries and the ability to add company-specific domains. New VPCs must be covered automatically. What should the solutions architect implement?

choices.text: DNS Firewall managed and custom lists via Firewall Manager, with query logs
GuardDuty DNS findings with EventBridge rules that add the offending IPs to security groups
Network ACLs on every subnet that deny outbound UDP and TCP 53 except to approved resolvers
AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with stateful domain rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall filters queries at the VPC Resolver, including AWS managed domain lists for malware and newly registered domains, plus custom block and allow lists. Firewall Manager applies DNS Firewall policies across accounts and automatically to new VPCs in scope, and Resolver query logging records what was blocked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network Firewall per VPC: can filter domains in traffic, but it's costly per VPC and doesn't use the managed DNS threat lists at the resolver. It's also more to run.
• NACLs on port 53: can't see domain names at all, and would break DNS to the VPC resolver.
• GuardDuty with SG updates: detective and after the fact. Blocking IPs doesn't stop resolution of new malicious domains.

Key takeaway: domain-level DNS blocking at scale → DNS Firewall with Firewall Manager.

stem: A global enterprise has a Transit Gateway in each of three Regions, each attached to dozens of VPCs, and an on-premises network connected via Direct Connect in each Region. The company wants a single, centrally managed hybrid connection strategy that reaches all Regions' Transit Gateways without provisioning a separate Direct Connect connection per Region. What should be used?

choices.text: VPC peering between the Transit Gateways in each Region, with one Region connected to Direct Connect
A Direct Connect gateway associated with each Region's Transit Gateway through transit VIFs
A single Direct Connect public virtual interface shared by the Transit Gateways in all Regions
A separate Site-to-Site VPN per Region terminating on each Region's Transit Gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway can associate with Transit Gateways in multiple Regions through a transit VIF, giving on-premises access to all Regions over the DX connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW peering via one Region: extra hops and complexity.
• Public VIF: reaches public endpoints, not VPCs.
• Separate VPNs: doesn't use Direct Connect.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway + TGWs.

stem: During a merger, Company A's VPC (10.0.0.0/16) and the newly acquired Company B's VPC (10.0.0.0/16) both need limited communication for a set of shared services, but re-addressing either VPC is not feasible in the short term. What is the recommended approach to enable this connectivity?

choices.text: Create a VPC peering connection and route the shared CIDR to each other's VPC
Update the route tables to send 10.0.0.0/16 traffic to the other VPC through a gateway
Use NAT (TGW with a NAT/proxy layer) for only the specific endpoints that must talk
Attach both VPCs directly to a Transit Gateway with route propagation enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overlapping CIDRs can't be routed directly. NAT (for example, a NAT or proxy layer with the TGW) translates only the specific endpoints that must talk, until re-IP is possible. PrivateLink is another option for specific services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering with the same CIDR: not allowed.
• Routing 10.0.0.0/16 to the other VPC: conflicts with local routes.
• TGW propagation: overlapping routes can't be resolved.

Key takeaway: overlapping CIDRs → translate (NAT) or expose services (PrivateLink).

stem: A company with 50 AWS accounts wants employees to sign in once and access only the specific AWS accounts and roles relevant to their job function, without creating IAM users in each account. Which service should be used?

choices.text: Amazon Cognito user pools federated to IAM in each of the 50 accounts
IAM users replicated across all accounts by a synchronization script
Cross-account IAM roles configured manually by each account owner
IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to groups for specific accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on and assigns permission sets to groups for specific accounts, which creates scoped roles in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito: for application users, not workforce AWS access.
• Replicated IAM users: long-term credentials and sprawl.
• Manual cross-account roles: inconsistent and hard to audit.

Key takeaway: workforce access across accounts → Identity Center.

stem: An engineer must block a single abusive IP range from reaching web servers in a public subnet while still allowing everyone else on 443. Responses to legitimate clients must keep working. The web servers' security group already allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the correct change?

choices.text: Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 rule from the security group and add allow rules for every other address range
Add a NACL outbound DENY for the range, since NACLs are stateful and will also block inbound
A lower-numbered NACL inbound DENY for the range, keeping ephemeral outbound
Add a DENY rule for the IP range to the web servers' security group above the existing allow rule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups are stateful and allow-only: they can't express 'everyone except X'. Network ACLs are stateless, support DENY, and evaluate rules in ascending number order, so a lower-numbered DENY for the abusive range takes effect before the broader ALLOW 443. Because NACLs are stateless, outbound rules must still allow ephemeral ports so responses reach legitimate clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG deny rule: security groups do not support deny rules.
• Allow-listing everyone else: impractical, and it hits the security group rule limits.
• Outbound NACL deny as if stateful: NACLs are stateless. An outbound rule does not block inbound requests, and it would only break responses.

Key takeaway: deny a specific range → NACL (ordered, stateless); allow-by-reference and stateful → security group.

stem: A global company needs to encrypt data in DynamoDB Global Tables replicated across three Regions using customer-managed keys, and wants each region's replica encrypted with a key that has the same key ID and key material across Regions to simplify operations. Which KMS feature should be used?

choices.text: AWS managed keys (aws/dynamodb)
Independent single-Region KMS keys created in each Region with the same alias
KMS multi-Region keys (primary plus replicas)
Client-side encryption with a shared secret stored in Secrets Manager in each Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS multi-Region keys share key material and ID across Regions, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another, which fits Global Tables with customer managed keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed keys: not customer managed.
• Independent keys with the same alias: different key material, so cross-Region decryption fails.
• Client-side encryption with a shared secret: complex and weaker key management.

Key takeaway: cross-Region encrypt/decrypt with one logical key → multi-Region keys.

stem: A company must continuously detect CVEs in 3,000 EC2 instances and ECR images across 40 accounts, rescan automatically when new CVEs are published, prioritize by network exposure, and avoid managing separate scanner agents. Most instances already run the SSM Agent. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector org-wide via a delegated administrator
AWS Config rules checking installed package versions, with findings aggregated in Security Hub
A third-party scanner AMI in each account, launched weekly by EventBridge to scan instances
GuardDuty Malware Protection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector continuously scans EC2 (using the SSM Agent, with no separate agent to manage) and ECR images, and automatically rescans when new CVEs appear. Its risk score factors in network reachability, and a delegated administrator enables and views it across the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config package-version rules: Config tracks configuration and isn't a CVE database, so you'd build the vulnerability logic yourself.
• Weekly third-party scanner: not continuous, adds infrastructure, and misses newly published CVEs between runs.
• GuardDuty Malware Protection plus basic scanning: malware isn't CVEs, and basic ECR scanning runs only at push without continuous rescans.

Key takeaway: continuous CVE management for EC2, ECR, and Lambda → Amazon Inspector, org-wide via delegated admin.

stem: After adding a new NACL rule to explicitly allow inbound traffic on port 443, a web application in a private subnet still cannot receive responses to outbound HTTPS requests it initiates to an external API. The security group only has an outbound allow-all rule and no inbound rules. What is the most likely issue?

choices.text: The private subnet's route table is missing a route to the internet gateway for response traffic
KMS encryption on the instance's EBS volume is blocking the HTTPS response
Stateless NACL outbound rules block the ephemeral ports used by return traffic
The security group needs an explicit rule for response traffic, since security groups are stateless

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless. Allowing inbound 443 isn't enough; outbound rules must allow ephemeral ports (1024-65535) for responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IGW route for a private subnet: not the issue and would make it public.
• EBS encryption: unrelated to network traffic.
• Security group return rules: SGs are stateful.

Key takeaway: NACL changes → check both directions.

stem: Two divisions in separate AWS accounts need to exchange sensitive files via S3, with a requirement that data is encrypted at rest with keys each division controls, and encrypted in transit, while access must be auditable and revocable per file exchange. Which design best satisfies all requirements with reasonable operational overhead?

choices.text: Use SFTP through AWS Transfer Family with static credentials shared between the divisions by email
Replicate the bucket to the other account with default encryption settings and no customer managed key
Make the bucket public and rely on short-lived presigned URLs to limit who can read each object
Cross-account bucket policy, SSE-KMS with a shared CMK, TLS-only condition, CloudTrail data events

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cross-account bucket policy grants the partner, SSE-KMS with a key whose policy grants both accounts controls encryption, an aws:SecureTransport condition enforces TLS, and CloudTrail records access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SFTP with shared static credentials: weak identity.
• Replication with default encryption: loses key control.
• Public bucket with presigned URLs: violates the requirement.

Key takeaway: cross-account sensitive sharing = bucket policy + KMS key policy + TLS + audit.

stem: A company running a fleet of on-premises VMware VMs needs to implement disaster recovery to AWS with sub-second replication and the ability to fail over entire servers within minutes, without re-architecting the application. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: AWS Backup
AWS Application Migration Service configured for one-time migration only
AWS DataSync
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers at block level to AWS, giving an RPO of seconds and failover within minutes, with non-disruptive drills.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Backup: periodic backups, not continuous replication.
• MGN one-time migration: for migrations, not ongoing DR.
• DataSync: file transfers, not server replication.

Key takeaway: server DR to AWS → Elastic Disaster Recovery.

stem: A company must retain compliance backups of RDS snapshots for 7 years, replicated to a separate AWS account and Region, with protection against accidental or malicious deletion even by account administrators. What should be implemented?

choices.text: S3 Lifecycle rules on exported snapshot files in another account, without Object Lock
RDS automated backups with retention raised to the 35-day maximum
AWS Backup cross-account, cross-Region copies with Vault Lock in compliance mode
Manual RDS snapshots copied by a cron script to another account every month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup copies to another account and Region, with Vault Lock in compliance mode, retain backups for 7 years and prevent deletion by anyone, including administrators.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 lifecycle without Object Lock: deletable.
• 35-day automated backups: too short.
• Cron script copies: fragile and deletable.

Key takeaway: long retention + immutable + cross-account → AWS Backup + Vault Lock.

stem: An e-commerce application experiences a sudden, sustained 5x increase in traffic during a flash sale that lasts for hours, and the current architecture uses a single large EC2 instance behind a load balancer. Which change best improves both resilience and cost-efficiency for this pattern?

choices.text: An Auto Scaling group of smaller instances across AZs that scales out with demand
Permanently run several copies of the large instance type behind a load balancer at all times
Scale up the single instance to a larger type ahead of each announced sale
Move to a single, larger instance in a different AZ with more available capacity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Horizontal scaling across AZs with an Auto Scaling group adds instances as demand grows, handling sustained 5x load without the single-instance ceiling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent copies: pays for peak capacity all year.
• Pre-sale vertical scaling: ceilings and downtime.
• Larger single instance: still a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: elastic scale-out beats bigger boxes.

stem: A company has implemented a warm standby DR strategy in a secondary Region with databases continuously replicated and a minimal application tier always running. During a recent regional failover test, RTO exceeded the target because scaling the application tier from minimal to full capacity took too long. What is the most effective way to reduce RTO without significantly increasing standing cost?

choices.text: Relax the RPO requirement so the team can focus the DR budget on improving recovery time
Move to a pilot light strategy so there is less standby infrastructure to scale during failover
Switch to multi-site active-active across both Regions, running full capacity at all times
Pre-configure and test aggressive scaling triggered by failover automation, and pre-warm key components

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The standby scales slowly because scaling isn't prepared. Pre-configuring aggressive scaling triggered by failover automation, and testing it, meets the RTO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relaxing RPO: doesn't help recovery time.
• Pilot light: even less standby capacity, so slower.
• Active-active: meets the goal but at much higher cost than needed.

Key takeaway: warm standby works only if scale-up is automated and tested.

stem: A company implemented a pilot light DR strategy where only the database is continuously replicated to the DR Region. During an actual regional outage, the recovery took 4 hours instead of the targeted 30 minutes because engineers had to manually launch EC2 instances, deploy application code, and reconfigure load balancers and DNS. What should be added to meet the RTO target on future failovers?

choices.text: Relax the RPO so the recovery process has more time to rebuild the application tier
Switch the database from continuous replication to periodic snapshots to simplify failover
Prebuilt AMIs or IaC for the app tier and automated, tested failover runbooks with DNS cutover
Remove the pilot light and rely on cross-Region backups, which recover faster than replicas

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pilot light keeps only data running, so the app tier must be built quickly. Prebuilt AMIs or IaC and automated, tested runbooks make that rebuild fast and reliable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relaxing RPO: RPO isn't the problem.
• Snapshots instead of replication: worsens RPO.
• Backups only: slower than pilot light.

Key takeaway: pilot light depends on automation for the missing tiers.

stem: A global trading platform requires near-zero RTO and RPO, with active user traffic served simultaneously from two Regions, and any single Region's failure must be invisible to end users. Which DR strategy should be implemented?

choices.text: Backup and restore with frequent cross-Region snapshot copies
Pilot light with the database continuously replicated
Warm standby with a scaled-down copy of the full stack
Multi-site active-active, serving traffic from both Regions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Near-zero RTO and RPO with both Regions serving traffic is multi-site active-active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Backup and restore: hours of recovery.
• Pilot light: minutes to hours to build capacity.
• Warm standby: faster, but not simultaneous full serving.

Key takeaway: near-zero RTO/RPO → active-active.

stem: An architect is choosing an EC2 Auto Scaling policy for a workload with a highly predictable daily traffic pattern (peaks every weekday at 9 AM) as well as occasional unpredictable spikes. Which combination of scaling approaches is most appropriate?

choices.text: Predictive scaling for the daily pattern plus target tracking for unexpected spikes
Scheduled scaling only, with capacity raised for the 9 AM peak every weekday and lowered each evening
Simple scaling policies only, since step adjustments react to each alarm quickly
Manual scaling adjusted each morning by an on-call engineer before traffic arrives

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling learns the daily pattern and adds capacity ahead of the 9 AM peak, and target tracking handles unexpected spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled only: misses unplanned spikes.
• Simple scaling: slower and coarser.
• Manual scaling: unreliable.

Key takeaway: known patterns → predictive; surprises → target tracking.

stem: A company runs its primary application stack in us-east-1 and a fully provisioned standby stack in us-west-2. It wants automatic DNS failover to the standby Region if health checks against the primary fail, without manual DNS changes. What should be configured?

choices.text: Simple routing pointing to the primary Region's endpoint, updated by a runbook during incidents
Route 53 failover routing with health checks on the primary endpoint
Weighted routing split 50/50 between both Regions
A CNAME record that the on-call engineer updates manually to the secondary endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing with a health check on the primary answers with the secondary record automatically when the primary is unhealthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing with a runbook: manual.
• 50/50 weighted: sends traffic to the standby all the time.
• Manual CNAME: slow.

Key takeaway: automatic DNS DR → failover records + health checks.

stem: A company wants its Amazon Aurora MySQL database's data to be available for near-real-time recovery in a secondary Region with an RPO of a few seconds, and the ability to promote the secondary to a full read/write cluster during a regional disaster. Which Aurora feature should be used?

choices.text: Cross-Region read replicas using MySQL binlog replication plus 15-minute snapshot exports
Aurora Global Database with sub-second lag and fast secondary promotion
Automated backups copied manually to the other Region each day
Aurora Serverless v2 in both Regions with auto-pause enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates to secondary Regions with typically sub-second lag and supports fast promotion, meeting an RPO of seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Binlog replicas plus snapshots: higher lag and slower recovery.
• Daily manual copies: RPO of a day.
• Serverless auto-pause: not a DR mechanism.

Key takeaway: cross-Region Aurora DR → Global Database.

stem: A company is comparing AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery against a traditional AMI-snapshot-based backup and restore approach for its on-premises fleet. Which factor most strongly favors choosing Elastic Disaster Recovery for a workload with a strict low RTO/RPO requirement?

choices.text: DRS requires applications to be re-architected as cloud-native services before they can be protected
Backup and restore provides automatic, non-disruptive failover testing at no additional cost
DRS replicates blocks continuously for an RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes; snapshot restore takes hours and manual steps
DRS costs much less to run continuously than storing periodic snapshots for the same servers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates blocks continuously (RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes), while snapshot-based backup and restore has larger RPO and slower recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Re-architecture required: DRS works with existing servers.
• Free automatic drills with backups: not true.
• DRS always cheaper: it adds continuous replication costs.

Key takeaway: continuous replication vs. periodic snapshots.

stem: An Auto Scaling group configured with a target tracking policy on CPU utilization is scaling out and then immediately scaling back in repeatedly (flapping), causing instability. What is the most likely misconfiguration and fix?

choices.text: Cooldown or instance warm-up is too short, so scaling acts before new instances affect the metric
The load balancer health check grace period is set to zero, so new instances are replaced immediately
The VPC does not have enough subnets, so scale-out attempts fail and are rolled back
The Auto Scaling group has no launch template, so launched instances are terminated right away

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the cooldown or instance warm-up is too short, the policy reacts before new instances contribute, causing repeated scale-out and scale-in (flapping).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Zero grace period: causes health replacements, not scaling flaps.
• Too few subnets: causes launch failures, not flapping.
• No launch template: the group couldn't launch at all.

Key takeaway: flapping → tune warm-up and cooldown.

stem: A company is designing its AWS Organizations structure and wants to apply different sets of guardrails to production workloads versus development/test workloads, while keeping billing and security tooling centralized. What is the recommended approach?

choices.text: Use resource tags to enforce environment-specific guardrails through tag-based IAM conditions, without OUs
Separate Production and Non-Production OUs, each with its own SCPs and dedicated accounts
Create one account per team with no OU structure and manage guardrails inside each account
Put all accounts in one OU and use IAM policies to distinguish production from non-production

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate Production and Non-Production OUs let different SCPs apply to each environment, with dedicated accounts per workload.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags only: can be changed by users and are weaker guardrails.
• No OU structure: can't apply policies at scale.
• One OU with IAM: IAM isn't an org-wide guardrail.

Key takeaway: environment guardrails → OUs + SCPs.

stem: A security team wants every member account in the organization to automatically forward GuardDuty findings to a centralized EventBridge event bus in the security account, so that automated remediation Lambda functions can act on findings from any account. What is the best way to architect this?

choices.text: A GuardDuty delegated administrator plus EventBridge routing of findings to a central bus
Lambda functions in each account that poll the GuardDuty APIs of every other account
A daily CSV export of GuardDuty findings from each account to a shared S3 bucket
CloudTrail Insights in each account forwarding unusual API activity to the security account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A GuardDuty delegated administrator aggregates member findings, and EventBridge rules in the administrator account route them to a central bus or targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling Lambdas: complex and fragile.
• Daily CSV: not near real time.
• CloudTrail Insights: not GuardDuty findings.

Key takeaway: org-wide security findings → delegated admin + EventBridge.

stem: A central networking team manages a set of subnets in a dedicated network account and wants application teams in 20 other accounts to be able to launch EC2 instances directly into those specific subnets, without copying or duplicating VPC resources into each account. What should be used?

choices.text: Recreate the VPC configuration in each of the 20 accounts with CloudFormation StackSets
Share the specific subnets with the other accounts (or the OU) through AWS RAM
Cross-account IAM roles that grant ec2:RunInstances into the network account's subnets
VPC peering from the network account's VPC to a VPC in each of the 20 accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC sharing through RAM lets participant accounts launch resources into the owner's subnets, while the network team keeps control of the VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreating VPCs: defeats central management.
• Roles into the network account: resources belong to the wrong account.
• Peering: separate VPCs, not shared subnets.

Key takeaway: central subnets for many accounts → RAM subnet sharing.

stem: A developer in a member account reports that even though their IAM policy explicitly allows s3:DeleteBucket, they receive an AccessDenied error. The organization's root OU has an SCP that denies s3:DeleteBucket for all accounts except those in the Backup-Exempt OU, and this account is in a different OU. What is the correct explanation and fix?

choices.text: The developer must attach an identical allow statement to the SCP so it matches the IAM policy
SCPs apply only to accounts directly under the root, not to accounts in nested OUs
SCPs cap permissions for the OU, so no IAM policy can grant a denied action
IAM policies take precedence over SCPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs set the maximum available permissions for accounts in an OU. If an SCP doesn't allow (or explicitly denies) s3:DeleteBucket, no IAM policy can grant it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Matching allow in the SCP: only if the org chooses to permit it; the developer can't fix it.
• Only direct children: SCPs apply through the OU hierarchy.
• IAM overrides SCPs: the opposite.

Key takeaway: effective permissions = IAM ∩ SCP.

stem: In a Control Tower landing zone, an auditor asks how the company prevents workload administrators from deleting CloudTrail logs that record their own actions. Which design BEST explains this?

choices.text: A dedicated Log Archive account, with preventive controls on members
IAM Identity Center permission sets exclude cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
Each workload account keeps its own trail in a local bucket protected by MFA Delete
The management account stores all logs so workload administrators can't sign in to it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower separates duties with dedicated accounts. The Log Archive account centrally stores organization CloudTrail and Config logs, and mandatory preventive controls (SCPs) stop member accounts from disabling or changing the logging setup. Workload administrators have no rights in the Log Archive account, so they can't erase evidence of their own actions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local trails with MFA Delete: the same account admins who are being audited own the bucket and can change settings.
• Logs in the management account: best practice is to keep the management account minimal. Log storage belongs in a separate, locked-down account.
• Removing DeleteTrail from permission sets: doesn't stop other ways to disable logging, such as deleting the bucket, and can be changed by whoever administers Identity Center.

Key takeaway: put audit evidence in a different account from the people being audited, and enforce it with preventive controls.

stem: A company with 60 accounts wants a single, queryable view of CloudTrail events across the entire organization for security investigations, without requiring each account team to manage their own trail configuration. What is the most operationally efficient design?

choices.text: An organization trail to a central Log Archive bucket, queried with Athena or CloudTrail Lake
VPC Flow Logs from every account, delivered to one bucket as the primary source for investigations
Export CloudTrail data from each account to an on-premises SIEM with no aggregation in AWS
Have each account team maintain its own trail and grant the security team read access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail delivers all accounts' events to a central Log Archive bucket, where Athena or CloudTrail Lake can query them without per-account setup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: network traffic, not API events.
• On-prem SIEM without aggregation: fragmented.
• Per-account trails: inconsistent and complex.

Key takeaway: org-wide API audit → organization trail.

stem: A large enterprise is deciding between building a custom multi-account landing zone using AWS Organizations APIs and CloudFormation StackSets versus adopting AWS Control Tower. Which factor most strongly favors Control Tower for this enterprise?

choices.text: Custom-built landing zones cost less than Control Tower at any scale, since there are no managed service fees
Control Tower removes the need for AWS Organizations by managing accounts on its own
Control Tower gives prebuilt baselines, controls, and Account Factory out of the box
Control Tower supports every custom governance requirement without any limitations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower provides prebuilt baselines, controls, and Account Factory quickly, but with less flexibility than a fully custom landing zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom always cheaper: not generally true, and it costs engineering time.
• Replaces Organizations: it's built on Organizations.
• Supports every custom need: it has limits.

Key takeaway: Control Tower trades flexibility for speed and standardization.

stem: A central network account owns a Transit Gateway that must be used by 50 spoke accounts in an Organization to attach their VPCs, without granting those accounts any other permissions in the network account. What is the correct way to share the Transit Gateway?

choices.text: Peer each spoke VPC directly with the network VPC instead of sharing the Transit Gateway
Create IAM users in the network account for each spoke team to manage their attachments
Have the network team create each spoke attachment after collecting VPC IDs from every team
Share the Transit Gateway through RAM with the organization so spoke accounts create their own attachments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sharing the TGW through RAM lets spoke accounts create their own attachments without being given any permissions in the network account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: loses the hub.
• IAM users in the network account: over-privileged and long-term credentials.
• Network team creates each attachment: slow and centralizes work.

Key takeaway: shared network resources → RAM.

stem: An enterprise is deciding between a highly centralized multi-account governance model versus a decentralized model where each business unit account has significant autonomy. Which tradeoff best characterizes the choice?

choices.text: There is no real tradeoff, because centralized governance is better in every dimension
Centralized gives consistency and easier audit but slows teams; decentralized is faster but inconsistent
Centralized governance removes the need for service control policies in member accounts entirely
Decentralized governance always results in lower AWS costs because teams right-size resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Centralized governance gives consistency and simpler audits but can slow teams. Decentralized gives agility but risks inconsistency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tradeoff: there is one.
• Removes SCPs: SCPs are central tools.
• Decentralized always cheaper: not guaranteed.

Key takeaway: governance is a tradeoff between control and autonomy.

stem: A newly created OU was supposed to inherit an SCP denying the use of non-approved Regions, but resources are being created in unapproved Regions within accounts moved into that OU. The SCP is correctly attached to the OU. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: Region restrictions cannot be enforced with SCPs and must be implemented in IAM policies
The account must be in the management account's OU for SCPs to take effect
SCPs do not apply to newly moved accounts until they are manually re-registered
A wrong aws:RequestedRegion condition, a broad allow, or missing global-service exemptions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply to all accounts in an OU. If resources still appear in unapproved Regions, the SCP logic is likely wrong: a bad aws:RequestedRegion condition, an allow that overrides nothing, or missing exemptions for global services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't enforce Regions with SCPs: they can.
• Must be in the management OU: the opposite; SCPs don't apply to the management account.
• Manual re-registration: not required.

Key takeaway: debug the SCP's conditions and structure.

stem: Application teams request new AWS accounts weekly. Each account must arrive with standard guardrails, a baseline VPC, security tooling, and team-specific customizations kept in Terraform, with no manual steps by the platform team. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A Config aggregator that detects new accounts and reports missing baseline resources
Control Tower Account Factory for Terraform (AFT), with account requests and customizations in Git
IAM Identity Center permission sets that grant each team rights to build its own baseline
Organizations CreateAccount from a script, followed by a manual checklist for guardrails and networking

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AFT extends Control Tower Account Factory with a GitOps workflow. Account requests are committed as Terraform, the account is vended and enrolled with Control Tower guardrails, and global and account-specific customizations (baseline VPC, security tools) are applied automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Script plus checklist: the manual steps are exactly what the platform team wants to eliminate, and they invite drift.
• Permission sets for self-build: gives access, not a consistent baseline. Each team would build it differently.
• Config aggregator: detects missing pieces after the fact. It doesn't provision anything.

Key takeaway: automated, customized account vending → Account Factory; Terraform-based customizations → AFT.

stem: A batch processing workload runs nightly, can tolerate interruptions with a 2-minute warning, and can checkpoint progress. The team wants to minimize compute cost. Which purchasing option is most appropriate?

choices.text: On-Demand Instances, so nightly runs are never interrupted and always finish on schedule
Dedicated Hosts, which give predictable capacity for long nightly batch runs
Standard Reserved Instances with 3-year terms for the nightly batch capacity
Spot Instances, relying on checkpointing to tolerate the 2-minute interruptions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Interruptible, checkpointed batch work gets the lowest cost from Spot Instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand: full price.
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive and for licensing or compliance.
• 3-year RIs: commit to capacity used only at night.

Key takeaway: interruptible + checkpointed → Spot.

stem: Finance wants to analyze two years of spend by service and cost-center tag, receive an alert when the forecast predicts a monthly overrun, and have a non-production account's EC2 instances stopped automatically if its budget is exceeded. Which combination meets all requirements?

choices.text: Cost Explorer for trends; Budgets with forecast alerts and a stop action
Trusted Advisor cost checks for trends, and Budgets alerts that email the team to stop instances
Pricing Calculator for trends, and Cost Anomaly Detection to stop instances when the budget is exceeded
CloudWatch billing alarms for forecasts, and Cost Explorer to stop instances when spend is exceeded

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost Explorer analyzes historical spend, grouped by service or cost allocation tag. AWS Budgets supports forecast-based alerts and budget actions, which can apply IAM or SCP policies or stop specific EC2 or RDS instances when a threshold is crossed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Billing alarms and Cost Explorer: billing alarms track estimated charges, not forecasts, and Cost Explorer cannot act on resources.
• Pricing Calculator and Anomaly Detection: the Pricing Calculator estimates planned architectures, not history. Anomaly Detection flags unusual spend but has no stop action.
• Trusted Advisor with email: Trusted Advisor isn't a trend tool, and email means manual action.

Key takeaway: history → Cost Explorer; thresholds, forecasts, and automated responses → Budgets and budget actions.

stem: A company wants weekly, organization-wide reports on security groups open to the internet, service quota usage near limits, idle load balancers, and underused EBS volumes, delivered to a central team, using AWS Business Support. Which service provides these checks directly?

choices.text: AWS Compute Optimizer with enhanced infrastructure metrics
AWS Config with managed rules for each check
AWS Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations
AWS Trusted Advisor with organizational view

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor checks span security (for example, open security group ports), service limits, fault tolerance, performance, and cost (idle load balancers, underutilized EBS). With Business Support or higher the full set of checks is available, and organizational view aggregates results across accounts for a central team.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute Optimizer: rightsizing recommendations for compute and EBS only. No security group or quota checks.
• Config managed rules: could cover some configuration checks, but not quota usage or idle-resource cost checks without significant custom work.
• Cost Explorer rightsizing: EC2 cost recommendations only.

Key takeaway: broad best-practice checks across security, cost, limits, and resilience → Trusted Advisor. Deep rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

stem: A company suspects several of its EC2 instances and EBS volumes are oversized relative to actual utilization, and wants machine-learning-based, specific right-sizing recommendations including recommended instance types based on historical utilization metrics. Which service should be used?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Compute Optimizer
Amazon S3 Storage Lens
AWS Budgets with usage alerts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization history with machine learning and recommends specific instance types and EBS configurations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: broad checks, fewer specific rightsizing recommendations.
• Storage Lens: S3.
• Budgets: spend alerts.

Key takeaway: ML rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

stem: A company has 900 buckets across 70 accounts. It wants organization-wide metrics on storage growth, the share of noncurrent versions, and incomplete multipart uploads, plus recommendations to cut cost, exported daily for analysis. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudWatch storage metrics per bucket, combined in a cross-account dashboard
Trusted Advisor S3 checks with organizational view
S3 Storage Lens organization dashboard with daily export
S3 Inventory in every bucket, queried with Athena and a custom QuickSight dashboard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storage Lens aggregates usage and activity metrics across accounts and Regions. It highlights cost-saving opportunities such as noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads, provides recommendations, and can export metrics daily to S3 for further analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Inventory plus Athena: possible, but you'd build the organization-wide aggregation, metrics, and recommendations yourself for 900 buckets.
• CloudWatch storage metrics: basic size and object counts, with no insight into noncurrent versions or incomplete uploads and no recommendations.
• Trusted Advisor: a few S3 checks (mainly permissions and versioning), not organization-wide storage analytics.

Key takeaway: organization-wide S3 usage visibility and optimization → S3 Storage Lens.

stem: A large enterprise wants to allocate shared AWS costs, like a central networking account's Transit Gateway or NAT Gateway charges, back to the specific business units that generate the underlying usage, for internal chargeback reporting. What is the most effective foundational strategy to enable this?

choices.text: Enforced cost allocation tags plus Cost Categories to split direct and shared costs
Calculate allocations manually in spreadsheets exported from the monthly invoices
Enable Cost Explorer and group costs by service, without introducing a tagging strategy
Rely on account-level consolidated billing, since each account maps to one business unit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enforced cost allocation tags attribute direct costs, and Cost Categories can split shared costs (such as TGW or NAT charges) across business units by rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spreadsheets: manual and error-prone.
• Group by service only: no business-unit view.
• Account-level only: shared accounts serve many units.

Key takeaway: shared cost allocation → tags + Cost Categories.

stem: Before approving a migration, leadership wants a shareable monthly cost estimate for a planned three-tier application, comparing On-Demand with a 3-year Savings Plan, two instance families, gp3 versus io2 storage, and 20 TB of monthly data transfer out. Which tool fits BEST?

choices.text: Cost Explorer forecasts based on the current account's spending history
AWS Pricing Calculator with grouped, shared estimates
Compute Optimizer recommendations for the planned instance families
AWS Budgets with a forecast

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Pricing Calculator models architectures that don't exist yet. You configure services, pricing models (On-Demand versus Savings Plans), storage types, and data transfer, group them, and share or export the estimate for approval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer forecasts: based on past spending. It knows nothing about an application that hasn't been deployed.
• Compute Optimizer: analyzes running resources' utilization, so there's nothing to analyze yet.
• Budgets: tracks and forecasts actual spend against thresholds after deployment.

Key takeaway: before deployment → Pricing Calculator; after deployment → Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Compute Optimizer.

stem: A company has variable, hard-to-predict compute usage across several instance families and is deciding between committing to Standard Reserved Instances versus Compute Savings Plans for a 1-year term. What is the key tradeoff to communicate to leadership?

choices.text: RIs discount slightly more but are tied to family/Region; Compute SPs span families, Regions, and services
Compute Savings Plans can be canceled at any time, while Standard RIs can only be exchanged, not canceled
Compute Savings Plans and Standard RIs are functionally identical except for how they appear on the bill
Standard RIs automatically apply across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, just like Compute Savings Plans do

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standard RIs give slightly larger discounts but are tied to instance family and Region. Compute Savings Plans apply across families, Regions, Fargate, and Lambda, which suits variable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cancel anytime: both are commitments.
• Identical: they differ in flexibility.
• RIs cover Fargate and Lambda: they don't.

Key takeaway: variable usage → Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A finance team notices an unexpected spike in daily spend in Cost Explorer but doesn't know which service or linked account caused it, and wants proactive alerts for unusual spending patterns in the future rather than manually reviewing dashboards. What should they configure?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
A CloudWatch billing alarm with a fixed dollar threshold
A manual daily review of Cost Explorer graphs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to spot unusual spend, identifies the service or account, and sends alerts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: optimization tips.
• Fixed billing alarm: doesn't identify the cause.
• Manual review: slow.

Key takeaway: unexpected spend → Cost Anomaly Detection.

stem: A holding company's AWS Organizations management account consolidates billing for 40 linked accounts. Leadership wants each subsidiary to see only its own detailed billing and usage data, while the central finance team retains visibility into all accounts' costs and can apply organization-wide Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discount sharing. What billing feature enables the automatic sharing of RI and Savings Plans discounts across the linked accounts?

choices.text: Discount sharing is disabled by default in Organizations and cannot be turned on for linked accounts
Consolidated billing shares volume tiers and, unless turned off, RI and Savings Plans discounts
Each linked account must buy its own Reserved Instances
Only the management account can benefit from Reserved Instance discounts purchased in the organization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consolidated billing combines usage for volume tiers and, unless disabled, shares RI and Savings Plans discounts across accounts. Subsidiaries can see their own costs, and sharing can be turned off per account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabled by default: sharing is on by default.
• Each account must buy its own: not required.
• Only the management account benefits: discounts are shared.

Key takeaway: consolidated billing shares discounts by default.

stem: A data processing cluster running on Spot Instances is experiencing frequent job failures because instances are being reclaimed mid-task without the application saving progress in time. The team must continue using Spot for cost savings. What should be implemented to reduce job failures?

choices.text: Switch every instance to On-Demand, since Spot interruptions cannot be reduced in practice
Disable Spot interruption notices to avoid the processing overhead of handling them
Handle the 2-minute notice, diversify types and AZs, and use capacity-optimized allocation
Raise the Spot maximum price to the On-Demand price, which prevents interruptions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Handling the 2-minute interruption notice (checkpoint and drain), diversifying instance types and AZs, and using a capacity-optimized allocation strategy reduce interruptions and their impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All On-Demand: gives up the savings.
• Disable notices: loses the warning.
• Higher max price: Spot interruptions aren't driven by your bid.

Key takeaway: design for Spot: diversify and handle notices.

stem: A company purchased Reserved Instances for a workload that ran in a single Availability Zone (Zonal RI) to guarantee capacity reservation, but the workload has since moved to using an Auto Scaling group spanning three AZs, and now the RIs are underutilized. What change should be made to maximize RI discount utilization going forward?

choices.text: RIs cannot be converted, modified, or resold
Cancel the Reserved Instances and switch the workload entirely to On-Demand pricing
Use Regional RIs, which apply across AZs and sizes in the family
Buy more Zonal RIs in each of the other two AZs to match the new footprint exactly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Regional RIs apply to usage in any AZ in the Region and across sizes in the family (size flexibility), fitting a workload that moved across AZs. Zonal RIs can be modified to Regional.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't modify: RIs can be modified (and Standard RIs sold).
• Cancel for On-Demand: RIs can't be canceled.
• More Zonal RIs: over-commits.

Key takeaway: flexibility across AZs → Regional RIs.

stem: A firm runs 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and wants identical VPC, logging, and IAM guardrail resources deployed to every current and future account in specific OUs, with updates rolled out centrally. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: AWS Config rules with auto-remediation in each account
A single CloudFormation stack deployed manually in each account
A Lambda function triggered by account creation that calls the CloudFormation API in each account
CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions targeting the OUs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed StackSets deploy to target OUs and automatically to new accounts added to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config remediation: fixes drift, not full baselines.
• Manual stacks: don't scale.
• Custom Lambda on account creation: reinvents StackSets.

Key takeaway: org-wide baselines → StackSets with auto-deployment.

stem: A team's CodePipeline deploys a CloudFormation stack to a production account from a pipeline in a shared tooling account. Deployments must not grant the pipeline broad IAM permissions in production. What should they configure?

choices.text: Grant the pipeline's IAM role AdministratorAccess in the production account
A scoped cross-account role plus a CloudFormation service role in production
Store production account root credentials in Secrets Manager for the pipeline
Move the pipeline into the production account instead of the tooling account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The pipeline assumes a narrowly scoped cross-account role in production that can only pass a CloudFormation service role, which CloudFormation uses to create resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Root credentials: never.
• Pipeline in production: couples tooling with production.

Key takeaway: cross-account deployments via scoped roles.

stem: A company self-manages an Apache Kafka cluster on EC2 for streaming ingestion and spends significant engineering time patching brokers and handling failover. Leadership wants to reduce operational overhead while keeping the Kafka API. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Keep Kafka on EC2 but add an Auto Scaling group
Migrate to Amazon MSK
Migrate to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and rewrite producers/consumers
Migrate to Amazon SQS standard queues

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka as a managed service, removing broker patching and failure handling while keeping Kafka APIs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG around self-managed Kafka: still self-managed.
• Kinesis: requires rewriting producers and consumers.
• SQS: different semantics.

Key takeaway: managed Kafka → MSK.

stem: A CloudFormation template needs to provision a third-party SaaS resource that has no native CloudFormation resource type, and the provisioning logic must run as part of stack create/update/delete lifecycle. What should the architect use?

choices.text: A CloudFormation macro
A CloudFormation custom resource backed by a Lambda function
An AWS Config rule with auto-remediation
A separate Systems Manager Automation document run manually after stack creation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Lambda-backed custom resource runs your code during stack create, update, and delete to manage resources CloudFormation doesn't support natively.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macro: transforms templates; doesn't call external APIs at deploy time.
• Config remediation: not provisioning.
• Manual SSM document: outside the stack lifecycle.

Key takeaway: unsupported resources → custom resources.

stem: A CodeBuild project's build stage takes 25 minutes because it reinstalls all dependencies from scratch on every build, slowing the CI/CD pipeline significantly. What is the most effective way to reduce build time?

choices.text: Run the build on a persistent EC2 instance
Enable CodeBuild caching (S3 or local) for dependencies
Split the pipeline into more parallel CodePipeline stages
Increase the CodeBuild compute type to the largest available size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild caching (S3 or local) keeps dependencies between builds, avoiding reinstalling everything each time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Persistent EC2 build server: more operations.
• More parallel stages: doesn't speed dependency installation.
• Bigger compute: faster but still reinstalls.

Key takeaway: repeated dependency installs → caching.

stem: An ECS service needs a database password injected at container start. The password must rotate every 30 days without redeploying tasks, each access must be auditable, and only this service's task role may read it. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: A rotating Secrets Manager secret referenced in the task definition
An environment variable in the task definition
A Parameter Store Standard parameter referenced in the task definition, rotated by a scheduled Lambda
An SSE-S3 encrypted S3 object downloaded by the container at startup with the task role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager provides managed rotation for supported databases. ECS task definitions can reference a secret in the secrets section, so the value is injected at container start. Every GetSecretValue call is logged in CloudTrail, and resource and IAM policies can restrict access to the specific role that retrieves it. After rotation, newly started tasks receive the new value without a task definition change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store with custom rotation: no managed rotation, so you'd write and maintain the rotation and database-update logic yourself.
• S3 object: not a secrets store. There's no rotation, and anyone with bucket access can read it.
• Plain environment variable: visible in the task definition, and rotation requires a redeploy, which violates the requirement.

Key takeaway: rotating credentials with audit → Secrets Manager. Static configuration → Parameter Store.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update fails partway through and CloudFormation automatically begins rolling back, but the rollback itself fails, leaving the stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. What is the correct next step?

choices.text: Edit the resource states in the console to match the template, then retry the update
Wait for CloudFormation to retry the failed rollback automatically after a delay
ContinueUpdateRollback, skipping resources that cannot roll back
Delete the stack and manually recreate all of its resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ContinueUpdateRollback resumes the rollback and can skip resources that can't be rolled back, returning the stack to a usable state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Editing states in the console: not possible.
• Automatic retry: doesn't happen.
• Delete and recreate: destructive.

Key takeaway: stuck rollback → ContinueUpdateRollback.

stem: An architect is designing a deployment strategy for a new microservice on ECS Fargate that must shift traffic gradually to a new task set and automatically roll back on CloudWatch alarm triggers, with minimal custom scripting.

choices.text: Deploy a new ECS cluster entirely and manually redirect Route 53 records
CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for ECS with linear traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback
Manually update the ECS service desired count and monitor logs
Use a rolling update deployment configuration in the ECS service directly with no CodeDeploy integration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS creates a replacement task set, shifts traffic gradually (linear or canary), and rolls back on CloudWatch alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• New cluster with manual DNS: slow and manual.
• Manual desired count: no traffic shifting.
• Rolling update without alarms: no automatic rollback.

Key takeaway: gradual ECS releases with rollback → CodeDeploy blue/green.

stem: A company wants to give developers self-service access to provision pre-approved, standardized architectures (e.g., a three-tier web app stack) without giving them direct IAM permissions to create arbitrary resources.

choices.text: Systems Manager Automation documents shared publicly
Grant developers IAM permissions scoped to CloudFormation CreateStack only
AWS Service Catalog with CloudFormation product templates
Give developers read-only console access and have them file tickets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog offers approved CloudFormation products that developers can launch themselves, using a launch constraint role instead of broad permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public SSM documents: not governed products.
• CreateStack permissions: developers can deploy anything.
• Tickets: not self-service.

Key takeaway: governed self-service → Service Catalog.

stem: An organization wants patching, inventory collection, and command execution automated and standardized across a fleet of 2,000 EC2 instances and on-premises servers, without installing per-tool agents for each function.

choices.text: AWS Config rules with automatic remediation actions
AWS Systems Manager (Patch Manager, Inventory, Run Command)
CloudFormation drift detection scheduled hourly
A cron job on each server pulling patches from a repository

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Systems Manager covers hybrid fleets: Patch Manager for patching, Inventory for software data, and Run Command for commands.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config remediation: compliance, not fleet management.
• Drift detection: for stacks, not servers.
• Cron jobs: unmanaged and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: hybrid fleet operations → Systems Manager.

stem: A company implemented warm standby DR with asynchronous database replication to a secondary region. After a real failover test, they found 45 minutes of transactions were lost, exceeding their 5-minute RPO requirement. What most directly caused this and what should be changed?

choices.text: Replication lag exceeded the RPO; use tighter replication such as Aurora Global Database with lag monitoring
The DR Region's Auto Scaling group did not scale up fast enough to absorb the failed-over traffic in time
The RTO was misconfigured, and increasing the standby instance size will reduce the data loss
The Route 53 health check interval was too long, so writes continued to the failed primary and were lost
S3 Cross-Region Replication was not enabled for the application's log bucket, so data was missing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Losing 45 minutes of data means asynchronous replication lag exceeded the RPO. Tighter replication (such as Aurora Global Database with lag monitoring) reduces data loss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Slow scaling: affects RTO, not lost data.
• RTO misconfigured: RTO isn't about data loss.
• Health check interval: affects failover timing, not replication lag.
• Log bucket CRR: unrelated to database data loss.

Key takeaway: data loss = RPO problem = replication lag.

stem: A financial services company requires near-zero downtime and near-zero data loss for a critical trading platform, and is willing to accept the operational complexity and cost of running full production capacity in two regions simultaneously. Which DR pattern fits?

choices.text: Pilot light with manual failover procedures documented in a regularly reviewed runbook
Multi-site active-active with near-real-time replication and latency-based routing
Warm standby with a scaled-down secondary environment ready to scale out
Backup and restore using AWS Backup with cross-Region copies every hour

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Near-zero downtime and data loss, with willingness to pay for it, points to multi-site active-active with near-real-time replication and latency-based routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light: minutes to hours of recovery.
• Warm standby: faster, but not near-zero.
• Hourly backups: an hour of data loss.

Key takeaway: strictest RTO/RPO → active-active.

stem: An internal reporting app (EC2, RDS for PostgreSQL, and S3 files) can tolerate an 8-hour RTO and a 24-hour RPO after a Regional disaster. The budget allows almost no standing cost in the DR Region, but recovery must be repeatable. Which strategy fits BEST?

choices.text: Pilot light: a continuously replicated RDS replica in the DR Region, with the app tier built on failover
Warm standby: a scaled-down copy of the full stack running in the DR Region at all times
Multi-site active-active across both Regions with Route 53 latency routing
Backup and restore: AWS Backup copies to the DR Region, S3 CRR, and IaC to rebuild the stack on demand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With hours of RTO and a day of RPO, backup and restore is sufficient and cheapest. Cross-Region backup copies of RDS and EC2 volumes and S3 replication protect the data, and infrastructure as code rebuilds the environment consistently when needed, with almost no standing compute cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light: a running cross-Region replica adds continuous cost to meet an RPO the business doesn't need.
• Warm standby: runs compute continuously, far exceeding the budget for this tolerance.
• Active-active: the most expensive option, justified only for near-zero RTO and RPO.

Key takeaway: match the DR strategy to RTO/RPO. Paying for faster recovery than required wastes money, and IaC is what makes backup and restore repeatable.

stem: A SaaS app runs in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-northeast-1. Users must reach the Region with the best network performance, traffic must avoid a Region whose application health check fails, and EU users must stay in the EU for compliance. Which Route 53 configuration meets all requirements?

choices.text: Geolocation for Europe, latency records with health checks for others
Weighted routing with equal weights and health checks on each Region's endpoint
Geoproximity routing with bias values tuned so EU users usually reach eu-west-1
Latency-based routing with health checks for all users

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance requires deterministic placement of EU users, which geolocation provides. Route 53 supports nested policies (for example, with Traffic Flow or alias records to latency sets), so non-EU users get latency-based routing, and health checks remove unhealthy endpoints from answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency-based for everyone: an EU user could be routed outside the EU if another Region measures faster, which violates compliance.
• Geoproximity with bias: routes by distance and bias, so it doesn't guarantee EU users stay in the EU.
• Weighted routing: ignores both user location and network performance.

Key takeaway: hard location rules → geolocation; performance → latency; combine them with nested records and health checks.

stem: A globally distributed e-commerce application needs a database that can be written to from multiple regions with active-active replication and automatic conflict resolution, to support business continuity if any single region fails.

choices.text: DynamoDB global tables
Aurora Global Database (single-writer secondary regions)
ElastiCache Global Datastore
RDS Multi-AZ with a single primary

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB global tables provide multi-Region, multi-active writes with automatic replication.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Aurora Global Database: one writer Region.
• ElastiCache Global Datastore: a cache with one primary.
• RDS Multi-AZ: single Region.

Key takeaway: multi-Region writes → DynamoDB global tables.

stem: A production RDS for MySQL database must fail over automatically within about a minute during an AZ outage, the application must keep using the same endpoint, and the team also wants to offload read-only reporting queries to already-provisioned standby capacity. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: A single-AZ instance with a read replica that is promoted manually during outages
A cross-Region read replica, promoted automatically when the primary AZ fails
A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, sending reporting queries to its standby instance
A Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two readable standbys and a reader endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys in different AZs. Failover is automatic and typically faster than a Multi-AZ instance deployment, applications keep using the cluster endpoint, and the reader endpoint lets reporting use the standby capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ DB instance: the standby is not readable, so reporting can't use it.
• Read replica promoted manually: failover isn't automatic, and promotion changes the endpoint.
• Cross-Region replica: RDS doesn't automatically promote a cross-Region replica for an AZ failure, and it adds unnecessary cross-Region lag.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ instance = HA only. Multi-AZ cluster = HA plus readable standbys. Read replicas = read scaling or DR with manual promotion.

stem: A healthcare company must retain copies of critical S3 objects in a separate AWS Region for regulatory business continuity purposes, with replication of new objects happening automatically and asynchronously.

choices.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR) only
Manually run the AWS CLI sync command nightly
S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
