S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects to a bucket in another Region (with Replication Time Control for SLA-backed timing if needed).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same-Region Replication: same Region.
• Nightly CLI sync: manual and delayed.
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads.

Key takeaway: copies in another Region → CRR.

stem: During a failover drill, Route 53 failover routing did not redirect traffic away from a primary endpoint that was clearly down at the application layer, even though the EC2 instances themselves were running and passing basic TCP checks. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: CloudWatch alarms were not attached to the Auto Scaling group, so the failure was not detected
The secondary record's TTL was set too low, so resolvers ignored it during the failover
Route 53 failover routing requires a manual record update and does not fail over automatically
The health check tested TCP connectivity rather than an application-level HTTP(S) endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A TCP health check passes as long as the port accepts connections, even when the application is failing. An HTTP(S) check on an application endpoint detects the failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alarms on the ASG: unrelated to Route 53 failover.
• Low TTL: helps failover, not detection.
• Manual update needed: failover routing is automatic with health checks.

Key takeaway: health checks must test the application, not just the port.

stem: A central security team must let a third-party auditing vendor's AWS account read specific S3 buckets and CloudTrail logs in the company's account, without creating long-lived IAM users or sharing access keys. What should they implement?

choices.text: Share the company's root account credentials temporarily during the audit
Make the buckets public with a bucket policy restricting access by source IP
A cross-account read-only role trusted by the vendor's account
An IAM user with an access key shared securely with the vendor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cross-account role with read-only access to specific buckets and logs, trusted only by the vendor's account (optionally with an external ID), gives temporary, auditable access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root credentials: never.
• Public buckets: exposes data.
• Shared access keys: long-term secrets.

Key takeaway: third-party access → cross-account role (with external ID).

stem: An application in a private subnet cannot reach an RDS instance in a different subnet of the same VPC, despite security groups allowing the traffic on port 3306 in both directions. Network ACLs are the default suspect. What is most likely misconfigured?

choices.text: The VPC route table is missing a route for the RDS subnet's CIDR range
The stateless NACL lacks inbound or outbound rules for the ephemeral response ports
Security groups are stateless and need a matching outbound rule for replies
The RDS instance needs a public IP address to be reachable from other subnets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups allow the traffic, so the stateless NACL is the likely blocker: it must allow the database port inbound on one side and ephemeral response ports on the other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing local route: VPC routes include local traffic automatically.
• Stateless SGs: SGs are stateful.
• Public IP: not needed inside a VPC.

Key takeaway: intra-VPC failures with correct SGs → check NACLs.

stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL database holds regulated data. Security requires encryption at rest with a key the company controls and can disable in an emergency, annual key rotation, key-usage logs, and the ability for a DR account to restore snapshots. Which approach meets all requirements?

choices.text: Use the AWS managed key aws/rds, which rotates automatically and can be shared with other accounts
A customer managed KMS key with rotation, shared via its key policy
Require SSL/TLS for all connections and encrypt backups with SSE-S3
Encrypt sensitive columns in the application and leave storage encryption disabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer managed key gives the company control: it can be disabled, rotation can be enabled, and usage is logged in CloudTrail. Snapshots encrypted with a customer managed key can be shared with another account once the key policy grants that account use of the key, which enables DR restores.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed key: rotates automatically, but you can't manage its key policy, so snapshots encrypted with it can't be shared cross-account, and you can't disable it.
• SSL/TLS plus SSE-S3: TLS protects data in transit, not at rest, and RDS storage isn't encrypted with SSE-S3.
• Column encryption only: leaves storage, logs, and backups unencrypted, which misses the at-rest requirement.

Key takeaway: control, disable, share cross-account → customer managed KMS key.

stem: An application running in a private subnet needs to call the S3 and DynamoDB APIs without traversing the public internet or requiring a NAT gateway, to reduce cost and improve security posture. What should be configured?

choices.text: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB
A VPC peering connection to the S3 service
Interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) for S3 and DynamoDB
A NAT gateway with a restrictive security group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB add private routes without NAT and without hourly charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering to S3: not possible.
• Interface endpoints: work but cost more; gateway is the simplest fit.
• NAT gateway: uses the internet path.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB privately → gateway endpoints.

stem: A public-facing web application is being targeted by a large-scale volumetric DDoS attack at the network layer as well as application-layer HTTP flood requests designed to exhaust backend resources. Which combination of services addresses both threats?

choices.text: Shield Advanced for L3/L4 attacks plus WAF rate-based rules for HTTP floods
Security groups with strict inbound rules that limit which ports are exposed
Shield Standard alone, which also mitigates application-layer HTTP floods
AWS WAF alone, which blocks both network-layer and application-layer DDoS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced L3/L4 DDoS protection (and L7 with WAF), while WAF rate-based rules block HTTP floods from abusive sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups: don't absorb DDoS.
• Shield Standard alone: doesn't stop HTTP floods.
• WAF alone: doesn't mitigate network-layer attacks.

Key takeaway: network + application DDoS → Shield Advanced + WAF.

stem: An application on EC2 in Account A must read an S3 bucket in Account A and write to a DynamoDB table in Account B. Security forbids long-term credentials on instances and requires least privilege. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: An instance profile role with AdministratorAccess in Account A, and a DynamoDB resource policy granting Account A full access
Access keys for a user in Account B stored in Secrets Manager in Account A and read at startup
An instance profile role in A for S3; the app assumes a scoped role in B (trusting A's role) for DynamoDB
An IAM user with access keys stored in the instance's environment variables, with permissions in both accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The instance profile gives the application temporary, automatically rotated credentials for its own-account resources. For the other account, it calls sts:AssumeRole on a role in Account B whose trust policy allows only Account A's instance role, and whose permissions allow only the needed DynamoDB actions on that table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM user keys: long-term credentials on the instance, which is forbidden.
• AdministratorAccess and full access: violates least privilege on both sides.
• Account B user keys in Secrets Manager: still long-term credentials. Storing them in a secret doesn't make them temporary.

Key takeaway: own account → instance profile; other account → AssumeRole into a narrowly scoped, trusted role.

stem: Two AWS accounts, Account A (data producer) and Account B (analytics consumer), need Account B's IAM role to read objects from an S3 bucket owned by Account A, following least-privilege principles.

choices.text: Apply only an IAM policy in Account B
A bucket policy in Account A granting the Account B role read access
Copy the data to a bucket in Account B every day through a scheduled export job
Grant Account B's root user full access to Account A through an IAM policy
Make the bucket public and rely on the bucket name being hard to guess

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account S3 access needs the bucket owner (Account A) to allow the external principal in a bucket policy, in addition to Account B's identity policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy in B only: A hasn't granted access.
• Daily copies: duplication and staleness.
• Root user full access: over-privileged.
• Public bucket: insecure.

Key takeaway: cross-account = resource policy + identity policy.

stem: A company wants RDS database credentials rotated automatically every 30 days without requiring application downtime or manual password updates in application configuration.

choices.text: Keep credentials in an encrypted config file and redeploy the application with new values each month
Rotate the RDS master password manually in the console every 30 days and update the application
Secrets Manager with automatic RDS rotation
Store credentials in Parameter Store as a SecureString parameter with a 30-day expiration policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates RDS credentials automatically on a schedule using managed rotation, and applications fetch the current value at runtime, so there's no downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypted config and redeploys: manual.
• Manual console rotation: error-prone.
• Parameter Store SecureString: no built-in rotation.

Key takeaway: automatic DB credential rotation → Secrets Manager.

stem: A company with 80 accounts in 3 Regions must continuously measure compliance against CIS AWS Foundations and PCI DSS, view one consolidated score per standard, and automatically route new critical findings to a ticketing system. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Artifact reports for CIS and PCI DSS downloaded monthly and reviewed by auditors
Security Hub org-wide with aggregation and EventBridge routing
Trusted Advisor security checks with organizational view and weekly email reports
Amazon Inspector CIS scans on EC2 instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub runs automated checks for standards such as CIS AWS Foundations and PCI DSS and shows a score per standard. A delegated administrator plus cross-Region aggregation gives one organization-wide view, and findings are emitted to EventBridge, where rules can route critical ones to ticketing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Artifact: provides AWS's own compliance reports (for example, AWS's PCI attestation), not checks of your accounts.
• Trusted Advisor: a limited set of security checks, not mapped to CIS or PCI controls, and weekly email isn't continuous routing.
• Inspector CIS scans: assess operating system configuration on instances, not AWS account-level controls across services.

Key takeaway: account-level standards compliance and a findings hub → Security Hub. AWS's own attestations → Artifact.

stem: An Auto Scaling group backs an API whose CPU utilization fluctuates unpredictably. The team wants the group to automatically maintain CPU utilization near a specific target value without manually defining scaling thresholds or step adjustments.

choices.text: Step scaling with multiple CloudWatch alarm thresholds
Target tracking on average CPU utilization
Scheduled scaling actions based on the time of day
Simple scaling policy with a single CloudWatch alarm

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking keeps average CPU near a target by adding and removing capacity automatically, which suits unpredictable load.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step scaling: more configuration and tuning.
• Scheduled: the load isn't time-based.
• Simple scaling: slower and coarser.

Key takeaway: hold a metric at a target → target tracking.

stem: A message processing system uses SQS standard queues to decouple producers from consumers. Occasionally a malformed message causes a consumer to fail processing repeatedly, blocking the queue's throughput. What should be added to improve reliability?

choices.text: Delete failed messages manually from the console when an operator notices them
Increase the visibility timeout to a very high value
A dead-letter queue with an appropriate maxReceiveCount
Switch to FIFO queues, which reject malformed messages at send time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A dead-letter queue receives a message after maxReceiveCount failed receives, removing poison messages so other messages keep flowing and failures can be inspected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual deletion: slow.
• Huge visibility timeout: delays everything.
• FIFO rejecting bad messages: FIFO doesn't validate content.

Key takeaway: poison messages → DLQ.

stem: A single incoming event (a new order) must trigger several independent downstream processes: inventory update, email notification, and analytics logging, each processed by separate systems at their own pace, with the ability to add new subscribers later without changing the publisher.

choices.text: Write the event to a single SQS queue that all three systems poll
A single Lambda function that calls all three systems in sequence
An SNS topic fanning out to a separate SQS queue per downstream system
The order service calls each downstream service synchronously over HTTP

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SNS fans out one event to multiple SQS queues, one per consumer, so each system processes independently with its own retries and buffering.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One queue polled by all: each message goes to only one consumer.
• One Lambda calling all: coupled failures.
• Synchronous HTTP calls: tight coupling.

Key takeaway: one event, many independent consumers → SNS to SQS fan-out.

stem: A multi-step order fulfillment workflow involves calling several Lambda functions in sequence, with conditional branching, retry logic on failures, and the need for visual tracking of each execution's state. Which service should orchestrate this?

choices.text: Amazon SQS with manually coded retry logic in each Lambda
AWS Batch
AWS Step Functions
Amazon SNS topic fan-out to all Lambdas simultaneously

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions coordinates Lambda steps with branching, retries, error handling, and visible state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS with manual retries: no workflow state.
• AWS Batch: for batch jobs.
• SNS fan-out: runs everything in parallel without order.

Key takeaway: multi-step workflows → Step Functions.

stem: During a flash sale, an application begins receiving ThrottlingException errors from the DynamoDB API and Lambda concurrent execution limits are being reached, causing failed requests. What is the most likely underlying cause and correct first step?

choices.text: S3 request rate limits have been exceeded on the bucket the Lambda functions read from
DynamoDB throughput and Lambda concurrency limits; raise quotas and review capacity settings
The Auto Scaling group's maximum size is too low for the flash sale traffic
The VPC has run out of available IP addresses for new Lambda network interfaces

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ThrottlingException from DynamoDB and hitting Lambda concurrency limits point to throughput and concurrency limits. Raise quotas or capacity (for example, on-demand mode) and review limits before events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 request limits: not the reported errors.
• ASG max size: Lambda and DynamoDB aren't in an ASG.
• IP exhaustion: shows as ENI errors, not throttling.

Key takeaway: read error names; they point to the limit.

stem: An application uses ElastiCache for Redis as a session store and cannot tolerate losing session data if the primary node fails. What configuration provides automatic failover to a replica with minimal data loss?

choices.text: ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes across AZs
Redis replication group with Multi-AZ and at least one replica
A single-node Redis cluster with daily manual snapshots
Redis with cluster mode disabled and no replicas

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Redis replication group with Multi-AZ and at least one replica fails over automatically to a replica, preserving session data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Memcached: no replication.
• Single node with snapshots: loses data since the last snapshot.
• No replicas: no failover.

Key takeaway: durable Redis sessions → replicas + Multi-AZ.

stem: Before a major product launch, an architect wants to gradually shift a small percentage of production traffic to a new version of a service running in parallel, monitoring error rates before committing to a full cutover, using DNS-level control.

choices.text: Route 53 geolocation routing to send one country to the new version
Route 53 simple routing pointed at the new version
Route 53 weighted routing
Route 53 latency-based routing between both versions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing sends a chosen percentage of DNS answers to the new version, which can be increased gradually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geolocation: splits by location.
• Simple routing: all or nothing.
• Latency: routes by performance.

Key takeaway: percentage shifts → weighted routing.

stem: An Auto Scaling group terminates instances during scale-in, but the application needs time to gracefully deregister from a service registry and flush in-flight requests before termination completes. What should be configured?

choices.text: A termination lifecycle hook
A longer health check grace period on the group
Instance termination protection on all instances
A longer cooldown period between scaling activities

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A termination lifecycle hook pauses termination so the instance can deregister and drain before it's terminated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grace period: about health checks after launch.
• Termination protection: blocks scale-in entirely.
• Cooldown: timing between scaling actions.

Key takeaway: graceful shutdown in ASGs → lifecycle hooks.

stem: Consumers of an SQS queue are processing messages slower than expected, and the same message is being received and processed multiple times by different consumers, causing duplicate side effects. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The queue is a FIFO queue, and FIFO queues do not support deduplication of received messages
Visibility timeout is shorter than processing time, so messages reappear
The consumers use long polling
Standard queues guarantee exactly-once processing, so this points to an SQS service defect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and another consumer receives it. Increase the timeout to exceed processing time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• FIFO: the queue here is standard.
• Long polling: reduces empty responses; doesn't cause duplicates.
• Exactly-once guarantee: standard queues are at-least-once.

Key takeaway: visibility timeout > processing time.

stem: An architect anticipates that a new product launch will require significantly more concurrent Lambda executions and EC2 On-Demand instances than the account's current default service quotas allow. What should be done well before the launch?

choices.text: Spread the workload across additional AWS accounts so each account stays under its default quotas
Review usage in Service Quotas and request Lambda and EC2 increases ahead of launch
Launch first and request quota increases once throttling appears, since increases apply within minutes
Move the EC2 portion to Spot Instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Review Service Quotas usage and request increases for Lambda concurrency and EC2 vCPUs ahead of launch, since increases can take time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More accounts: complexity.
• Request after throttling: failures during launch.
• Spot: may not be available and doesn't remove quota limits.

Key takeaway: plan quotas before demand.

stem: A batch analytics workload performs heavy in-memory data processing on large datasets and is currently running on general-purpose M-family instances, frequently hitting memory limits before CPU is fully utilized. What should the architect do to improve performance cost-effectively?

choices.text: Switch to a storage-optimized instance family such as I-family
Move the workload to a compute-optimized instance family such as C-family
Move the workload to a memory-optimized instance family such as R-family
Increase the number of general-purpose instances without changing the family

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Heavy in-memory processing benefits from memory-optimized R instances, with more memory per vCPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage-optimized: for local disk I/O.
• Compute-optimized: less memory per vCPU.
• More general-purpose instances: doesn't fix memory per instance.

Key takeaway: match instance family to the bottleneck.

stem: A transactional database workload requires consistent sub-millisecond latency and very high, predictable IOPS (64,000+) that must not degrade under sustained load. Which EBS volume type should be selected?

choices.text: gp3
st1 (throughput optimized HDD)
sc1 (cold HDD)
io2 Block Express

explanation:
Why this is correct:
io2 Block Express provides very high, consistent IOPS with sub-millisecond latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3: tops out at 16,000 IOPS per volume.
• st1 and sc1: HDD for throughput, not IOPS.

Key takeaway: extreme consistent IOPS → io2 Block Express.

stem: An application experiences a high cache-miss penalty because on a miss it must query the database directly, and the team wants the cache to always contain frequently accessed data populated on-demand as requests occur.

choices.text: Lazy loading (cache-aside)
Write-through caching on every database write
Write-behind caching with delayed database writes
No cache; add read replicas for the hot data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lazy loading populates the cache on demand after a miss, so the cache fills with data that's actually requested.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Write-through: fills the cache on writes, including rarely read data.
• Write-behind: delays database writes.
• No cache: doesn't address misses.

Key takeaway: populate on demand → cache-aside.

stem: An IoT platform ingests millions of time-stamped sensor readings per minute and needs to run fast time-range aggregation queries at scale, with automatic data lifecycle management for aging out old data. Which purpose-built database fits best?

choices.text: Amazon Timestream
Amazon Neptune
Amazon DynamoDB with a single partition key
Amazon QLDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Timestream is a purpose-built time-series database with fast time-range queries and built-in aggregation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neptune: graph.
• DynamoDB single partition key: hot partitions and no time-series functions.
• QLDB: ledger.

Key takeaway: time-series data → Timestream.

stem: Users report intermittent slow response times on a distributed microservices application, but aggregate CloudWatch metrics show no obvious single bottleneck. The team needs to pinpoint which specific service call in a request chain is causing latency.

choices.text: Add more CloudWatch alarms on per-service CPU utilization
Enable VPC Flow Logs and correlate request timestamps across services manually
Enable AWS X-Ray tracing across the services and review segment latencies
Increase CloudWatch metrics to 1-second high resolution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces individual requests across services and shows segment latencies, revealing where intermittent slowness occurs that averages hide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More CPU alarms: don't locate slow calls.
• Flow logs and manual correlation: slow and imprecise.
• 1-second metrics: still aggregates.

Key takeaway: find slow hops in distributed systems → tracing.

stem: During flash sales, the web tier receives 20x normal orders, and the order-processing tier (EC2, about 2 seconds per order) falls behind and drops requests. Orders must never be lost, customers can receive confirmation by email later, and processing must scale with the backlog. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Vertically scale the processors to the largest instance type during sales
Scale the processing tier on CPU utilization and add retries in the web tier
Put a Network Load Balancer between the tiers and raise the processors' connection timeouts
Write orders to SQS and scale the processors on queue depth (backlog per instance)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A queue decouples intake from processing. Orders are stored durably in SQS the moment they arrive, so a slow backend no longer causes drops. Scaling the consumers on backlog per instance (queue depth ÷ instances) adds capacity in proportion to the actual work waiting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB and longer timeouts: requests still wait synchronously and are lost when the backend is saturated.
• CPU scaling with retries: CPU lags the real backlog, and retries amplify load during the spike.
• Vertical scaling: has a ceiling, requires downtime to resize, and still drops requests beyond that ceiling.

Key takeaway: when work can be asynchronous, queue it and scale consumers on backlog, not CPU.

stem: A read-heavy application currently sends 100% of reads to a single RDS primary, causing latency spikes during peak hours. Adding read replicas will reduce primary load, but the team is concerned about read replicas returning slightly stale data. What is the correct tradeoff to communicate?

choices.text: Read replicas replace the primary for reads and writes, so the primary can be downsized
Replication is asynchronous, so reads may be slightly stale in exchange for scale
Read replicas return fully consistent data with zero lag
Replica lag can be eliminated entirely by adding more read replicas to spread the load

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas use asynchronous replication, so reads may be slightly stale, in exchange for offloading and scaling reads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicas handle writes: they're read-only.
• Zero lag: not guaranteed.
• More replicas remove lag: they don't.

Key takeaway: read replicas trade freshness for scale.

stem: A media company delivers video content to a global audience and wants to reduce latency for content delivery while also improving performance of dynamic, non-cacheable API requests routed to origin servers across regions.

choices.text: CloudFront for both static and dynamic traffic
Route 53 latency-based routing to regional endpoints, without a CDN or accelerator
CloudFront for cached video; Global Accelerator for the dynamic API
Global Accelerator for both the cacheable video and the non-cacheable API traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches video at the edge. Global Accelerator speeds up dynamic, non-cacheable API traffic by routing it over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront for both: works, but Global Accelerator is the purpose-built fit for non-HTTP-cacheable APIs with static IPs.
• Route 53 only: no caching or network acceleration.
• Global Accelerator for video: no caching.

Key takeaway: cacheable → CloudFront; dynamic acceleration → Global Accelerator.

stem: An application running on EC2 with attached EBS volumes shows disk-bound performance issues, with CloudWatch showing high VolumeQueueLength and throughput far below the instance's advertised network bandwidth. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The subnet has run out of IP addresses, which slows EBS attachment traffic
The instance isn't EBS-optimized or exceeds its EBS bandwidth
The security group is throttling traffic between the instance and EBS
The instance's placement group type limits its EBS throughput

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High VolumeQueueLength with capped throughput suggests the instance's EBS bandwidth is the limit, for example because it isn't EBS-optimized or its type has limited EBS bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Subnet IPs: unrelated to EBS I/O.
• Security groups: don't apply to EBS traffic.
• Placement group: doesn't limit EBS bandwidth.

Key takeaway: EBS performance is also limited by the instance.

stem: A high-traffic application uses DynamoDB as its primary data store and needs microsecond read latency for a small set of extremely hot keys accessed millions of times per minute, beyond what DynamoDB alone typically delivers.

choices.text: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode alone
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached placed in front of DynamoDB manually with custom cache invalidation logic as the only viable option
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB Global Tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond reads and minimal code changes (DynamoDB-compatible API).

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: capacity mode, not microsecond reads.
• Memcached with custom logic: more work.
• Global Tables: multi-Region replication.

Key takeaway: microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.

stem: A tightly-coupled HPC simulation workload requires low-latency, high-throughput networking between EC2 instances to minimize inter-node communication overhead during MPI jobs. What should the architect configure?

choices.text: A cluster placement group with instances that support enhanced networking
Standard On-Demand instances with no placement group
A spread placement group across multiple Availability Zones
A partition placement group intended for large distributed workloads like Hadoop

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cluster placement group packs instances close together in one AZ for low latency and high throughput, and enhanced networking (ENA or EFA) boosts it further.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No placement group: less predictable latency.
• Spread: separates instances for resilience.
• Partition: for large distributed stores.

Key takeaway: tightly coupled HPC → cluster placement group.

stem: An S3 bucket stores millions of objects with highly unpredictable and changing access patterns; some objects are accessed frequently for weeks then never again, while others are accessed sporadically. The team wants automatic cost optimization without manual lifecycle rule tuning per object.

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Deep Archive for all objects
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access for all objects
Manually crafted lifecycle rules moving objects to Glacier after exactly 30 days for every object

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on usage, with no retrieval fees for its automatic tiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deep Archive for all: slow retrieval.
• Standard-IA for all: retrieval fees for hot objects.
• Fixed 30-day rules: wrong for unpredictable patterns.

Key takeaway: unknown access patterns → Intelligent-Tiering.

stem: An architect notices high data transfer costs on the monthly bill and finds that application servers in one AZ are frequently calling a database in another AZ within the same VPC, and that a NAT gateway is processing significant traffic to reach S3 from private subnets. Which two changes would most reduce these costs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for all buckets to reduce regional transfer charges
Add an S3 gateway endpoint so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway
Keep app and database resources AZ-affine to cut cross-AZ traffic
Move all resources into a single Availability Zone and accept reduced redundancy
Increase the NAT gateway's bandwidth allocation to lower per-GB processing cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A gateway endpoint removes S3 traffic from the NAT gateway (no processing charges), and keeping app and database resources in the same AZ reduces cross-AZ transfer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: adds cost.
• Single AZ: sacrifices resilience.
• NAT bandwidth: doesn't change per-GB charges.

Key takeaway: cut transfer costs: endpoints and AZ affinity.

stem: A company wants a monthly review that finds idle load balancers, underutilized EBS volumes, and unassociated Elastic IPs across 50 accounts, and also gets rightsizing recommendations for EC2 instances based on memory and CPU usage. Which combination fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Budgets for idle resources, and Pricing Calculator for rightsizing
Trusted Advisor cost checks plus Compute Optimizer
Cost Explorer forecasts for idle resources, and Trusted Advisor for memory-based rightsizing
Compute Optimizer for idle load balancers and Elastic IPs, and Budgets for rightsizing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor's cost checks flag idle load balancers, underutilized EBS volumes, and unassociated Elastic IPs, and organizational view covers all accounts. Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization history, including memory when the CloudWatch agent publishes it, to recommend EC2 sizes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets and Pricing Calculator: neither finds idle resources or recommends sizes from utilization.
• Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor for memory rightsizing: forecasts don't identify idle resources, and Trusted Advisor's checks don't use memory metrics.
• Compute Optimizer for load balancers and EIPs: its scope is compute resources and EBS, not idle load balancers or Elastic IPs.

Key takeaway: waste detection → Trusted Advisor; utilization-based rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

stem: A company is considering committing to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan for significant discounts but is concerned about long-term flexibility if their architecture changes significantly, versus a 1-year commitment with a smaller discount. What is the correct tradeoff?

choices.text: 3-year gives a bigger discount but less flexibility if usage shifts; 1-year is the opposite
1-year Savings Plans always provide a greater discount than 3-year plans for the same commitment
A 3-year Savings Plan can be cancelled at any time without penalty if usage patterns change
The discount is the same for 1-year and 3-year terms; only the payment schedule differs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A 3-year term gives a bigger discount but locks in spend longer. 1-year is less discounted but more flexible if usage shifts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1-year bigger discount: the opposite.
• Cancel anytime: not allowed.
• Same discount: longer terms discount more.

Key takeaway: longer commitment = more discount, less flexibility.

stem: A company operates a small self-managed relational database cluster on EC2 that requires significant DBA time for patching, backups, and failover configuration. Leadership wants to reduce total cost of ownership including labor, and is open to a managed alternative with similar SQL compatibility.

choices.text: Move the database to larger EC2 instances
Migrate to Amazon S3 as the primary transactional data store to remove database administration
Keep the self-managed cluster but add more EC2 instances to improve redundancy
Migrate to Aurora or RDS for managed patching, backups, and failover

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora or RDS handle patching, backups, and failover, removing DBA toil.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger EC2: same toil.
• S3 as a transactional store: not a relational database.
• More self-managed instances: more toil.

Key takeaway: reduce database operations → managed databases.

stem: Petabytes of compliance recordings must be kept for 7 years and must not be deleted early by anyone. They are almost never read, and retrieval within 48 hours is acceptable. Recordings land in S3 Standard. Which design is MOST cost-effective while meeting the retention rule?

choices.text: Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier and a delete-deny SCP
Lifecycle to S3 Standard-IA with Versioning and MFA Delete enabled
Lifecycle to Deep Archive plus Object Lock compliance mode
Lifecycle to Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a bucket policy denying deletes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, and its standard retrieval within 12 hours (bulk within 48) fits the access pattern. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion or retention shortening by any user, including root, until the retention period ends.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flexible Retrieval with a bucket policy: costs more than Deep Archive, and bucket policies can be changed by administrators, so they don't guarantee retention.
• Standard-IA with MFA Delete: far more expensive for petabytes, and MFA Delete can be disabled by the bucket owner.
• Intelligent-Tiering with an SCP: adds per-object monitoring fees for data with a known access pattern, and SCPs can be changed by the management account.

Key takeaway: a known 'never read' pattern → direct lifecycle to Deep Archive; 'no one can delete' → Object Lock compliance mode.

stem: A company streams Lambda function logs through a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter into a Kinesis Data Stream for centralized analysis. During a traffic spike, engineers notice gaps in the centralized log data in Kinesis, even though CloudWatch Logs Insights queries run directly against the Lambda log group show every entry present for that period. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Logs Insights caches query results
Subscription filters only work for Lambda functions with reserved concurrency configured
The subscription filter's IAM role is missing kms:Decrypt on the log group key
The function's log retention policy deleted the older events before delivery
Too few Kinesis shards, causing throttling and dropped records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A stream with too few shards throttles writes from the subscription filter during spikes, so records are delayed or dropped. Add shards or use on-demand capacity mode.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights caching: unrelated to delivery.
• Reserved concurrency requirement: not a requirement.
• kms:Decrypt: would fail consistently, not only during spikes.
• Retention: doesn't delete events before delivery.

Key takeaway: spike-related delivery gaps → downstream capacity.

stem: A company runs a stateless containerized API on Amazon ECS and requires zero-downtime deployments plus the ability to instantly revert to the previous version if error rates spike after a release, without waiting to redeploy the old task definition. Which ECS deployment approach best satisfies this?

choices.text: ECS rolling update with minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 200
Replace task definitions one at a time manually in the ECS console
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS with two target groups
An all-at-once deployment through CodeDeploy with alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS runs a replacement task set behind a second target group, switches traffic, and can shift back instantly to the original.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling update: no instant revert to the old task set.
• Manual replacement: slow and error-prone.
• All-at-once with alarms: no instant rollback path.

Key takeaway: instant revert → blue/green.

stem: A company wants to validate, in a controlled and safe manner, that its multi-AZ Auto Scaling application correctly reroutes traffic and self-heals within its target RTO if an entire Availability Zone becomes unavailable, without waiting for a real outage. Which approach is best suited to this validation?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that reports on Availability Zone health after an outage occurs
Manually terminate every instance in one AZ during production business hours
Wait for CloudWatch anomaly detection to flag the condition if it happens naturally
An AWS Fault Injection Service AZ-impairment experiment with stop conditions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An AWS Fault Injection Service experiment that simulates AZ impairment, with stop conditions, safely tests recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rule: reports after the fact.
• Manual termination in production hours: uncontrolled.
• Waiting for a real event: no validation.

Key takeaway: test resilience safely → FIS with stop conditions.

stem: A company runs a critical Amazon RDS for MySQL database and wants to test a major engine version upgrade against production traffic patterns, then cut over with minimal downtime and a straightforward rollback path if problems appear immediately after cutover. Which native AWS approach best fits?

choices.text: Export a snapshot, restore it to a new instance, upgrade it, and repoint the application
RDS Blue/Green Deployments with a managed switchover
An in-place engine upgrade during a scheduled maintenance window
Create a read replica, upgrade and promote it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a synchronized staging (green) environment for the upgrade, then switch over with minimal downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snapshot restore and repoint: data diverges and downtime.
• In-place upgrade: no safe testing.
• Replica upgrade and promote: more manual and less controlled.

Key takeaway: safe major upgrades → RDS Blue/Green.

stem: On-call engineers receive separate pages for high CPU, high latency, and 5xx errors on the same service, often all at once. The team wants one page only when latency and 5xx errors are both alarming, but wants a warning ticket, not a page, for CPU alone. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: A paging composite alarm on latency AND 5xx
Longer evaluation periods on all three alarms so they fire less often
One alarm on a metric math sum of CPU, latency, and 5xx with a combined threshold
Anomaly detection bands on all three metrics, each paging on-call

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Composite alarms evaluate other alarms' states with AND/OR/NOT logic, so paging only happens when customer impact (latency plus errors) is confirmed. The CPU alarm stays useful as a non-paging signal routed to a ticketing topic, and the underlying alarms can suppress their own notifications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection on all three: changes the thresholds but still pages three times.
• Summing unrelated metrics: CPU percent, milliseconds, and error counts have different units, so a combined threshold is meaningless.
• Longer evaluation periods: delays alerts without reducing duplication.

Key takeaway: page on symptoms that matter (combined with composite alarms), and route causes such as CPU to lower-urgency channels.

stem: A company uses AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate on-premises servers into a recovery Region. During a quarterly DR drill, recovery instances launch successfully, but the team discovers that configuration drift had made the drill environment behave differently from production, and this was only caught during the live drill itself. What should the team change to prevent this going forward, consistent with operational excellence practices?

choices.text: Test DR only after major application releases, when configuration drift is most likely
Reduce the frequency of DR drills to lower the operational load on the team
Stop drills, since healthy replication lag metrics already confirm recovery readiness
Frequent, non-disruptive DRS recovery drills with automated post-launch validation tests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Frequent, non-disruptive DRS drills with automated post-launch validation catch configuration problems before a real disaster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only after major releases: drift happens anytime.
• Fewer drills: less confidence.
• Replication metrics alone: don't prove recovery works.

Key takeaway: practice recovery regularly.

stem: A company deploys a legacy stateful application to on-premises servers using AWS CodeDeploy. Deployments are restricted to an overnight maintenance window, capacity reduction during business hours must never occur, but a temporary outage during the designated overnight window is acceptable. Which CodeDeploy deployment configuration minimizes total deployment time for this scenario?

choices.text: OneAtATime
A custom configuration requiring a 90% minimum healthy percentage
HalfAtATime
AllAtOnce

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With a stateful legacy app and an overnight maintenance window, AllAtOnce deploys to every server at once within the window, which is simplest and fastest here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OneAtATime: may not finish within the window.
• 90% healthy: impractical for this app.
• HalfAtATime: still mixed versions of a stateful app.

Key takeaway: deployment config depends on the app and window.

stem: A CloudWatch alarm was configured on a custom application metric published with an InstanceId dimension. After the Auto Scaling group cycles instances during normal scale-in and scale-out events, the alarm frequently shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA and fails to alert on genuine problems, even though the application remains healthy and continues publishing metrics under new instance IDs. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase the number of evaluation periods on the alarm so new instances have time to report
Set the alarm to treat missing data as breaching
Alarm on an aggregate metric not tied to InstanceId
Switch the alarm's statistic from Average to a percentile such as p90

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An alarm on a per-InstanceId metric breaks when instances are replaced. Alarm on an aggregate metric (for example, by AutoScalingGroupName or no instance dimension).

Why the other options are wrong:
• More periods: still tied to old instances.
• Missing data as breaching: false alarms.
• Percentile: doesn't fix the dimension.

Key takeaway: alarm on fleet-level metrics for dynamic fleets.

stem: A company must store thousands of static application configuration values across many microservices at minimal cost, with only a small number of database credentials requiring automatic rotation every 24 hours. Which combination is the most cost-effective while still meeting all requirements?

choices.text: Store every value, static or rotating, in Secrets Manager for consistency
Store all values as KMS-encrypted objects in Amazon S3
Parameter Store SecureString for static values; Secrets Manager for rotating DB credentials
Store everything in Parameter Store and write custom rotation Lambda functions for the credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameter Store SecureString handles thousands of static values cheaply, and Secrets Manager handles the few secrets that need rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All in Secrets Manager: costly.
• KMS objects in S3: no parameter management.
• Custom rotation in Parameter Store: reinvents Secrets Manager.

Key takeaway: static config → Parameter Store; rotating secrets → Secrets Manager.

stem: A security team enabled Amazon Inspector across the organization and confirms EC2 instance vulnerability scanning is working, but container images pushed to Amazon ECR are not being scanned for vulnerabilities. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The pipeline's IAM role lacks ecr:PutImage
Amazon Inspector supports EC2 and Lambda scanning but does not scan container images
Inspector ECR scanning isn't enabled for those repositories
Amazon GuardDuty must be enabled first before Inspector can scan ECR images

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector's ECR (enhanced) scanning must be enabled for the repositories. EC2 scanning working doesn't mean ECR scanning is on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ecr:PutImage: affects pushes, not scanning.
• Inspector can't scan images: it can.
• GuardDuty prerequisite: not required.

Key takeaway: enable scanning per resource type.

stem: A company runs a fleet of stateless EC2 instances behind an Auto Scaling group and a separate fleet of stateful, singleton EC2 instances hosting a legacy application with no redundancy to fail over to. Both fleets must apply monthly OS security patches with minimal risk of extended downtime. Which strategy is most appropriate for the stateful singleton fleet using Systems Manager?

choices.text: Rely on OS-level unattended upgrades, which apply patches safely without orchestration
Exclude the singleton instances from patching
Patch Manager in an off-peak window, then validate app health
Replace each singleton instance monthly from a freshly patched AMI, like the stateless fleet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For singleton stateful instances, Patch Manager in an off-peak maintenance window, followed by application health validation, limits disruption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unattended upgrades: uncontrolled reboots.
• Excluding them: leaves vulnerabilities.
• Monthly replacement: risky for stateful singletons.

Key takeaway: stateful servers need scheduled, validated patching.

stem: A company wants a centralized, policy-driven backup solution across EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS resources spanning multiple AWS accounts, with backups copied to a separate, logically isolated backup account to protect against ransomware or accidental account compromise. Which approach best meets this?

choices.text: Org-wide AWS Backup policies with cross-account copies to a Vault Lock vault
AWS DataSync jobs that copy nightly exports into another account's S3 bucket
Each service's native snapshot feature configured separately in every account
The default 7-day RDS automated backup retention in each account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Organization-wide AWS Backup policies centrally define plans for EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS, with cross-account copies to a vault protected by Vault Lock.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataSync exports: not backups.
• Per-service snapshots: inconsistent.
• 7-day defaults: insufficient.

Key takeaway: central backup governance → Backup policies.

stem: A European company must ensure that no S3 buckets or RDS instances are ever created outside the eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 Regions across its entire AWS Organization, to satisfy a data residency requirement. The company wants to prevent the action rather than merely detect it afterward. What should they implement?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that flags and reports resources created in unapproved Regions
An IAM permissions boundary on each user restricting allowed Regions
An OU-level SCP that denies these actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not an approved Region
An EventBridge rule that deletes any resources created in other Regions automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An OU-level SCP denying the actions when aws:RequestedRegion isn't an approved Region prevents creation everywhere in the OU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rule: detective.
• Permissions boundaries: per user, easy to miss.
• EventBridge deletion: after the fact.

Key takeaway: prevent Region usage → SCP.

stem: A data lake with 4 PB across 200 buckets in 30 accounts may contain unmasked SSNs and card numbers. The company wants continuous, cost-controlled discovery across all accounts, plus a custom identifier for its internal employee ID format. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Config rules that flag buckets without default encryption as containing PII
Comprehend PII detection in Lambda for every object
Macie automated discovery with a custom data identifier
Daily full Macie classification jobs over every object in all 200 buckets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie is built for discovering sensitive data in S3. Automated sensitive data discovery samples objects continuously across the estate at controlled cost, a delegated administrator manages all member accounts, and custom data identifiers (regex plus keywords) detect company-specific formats such as employee IDs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily full jobs: rescanning 4 PB daily is very expensive and unnecessary for estate-wide visibility.
• Comprehend in Lambda: custom plumbing, it reprocesses the whole backlog, and it has no bucket-level inventory or findings management.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status says nothing about whether PII is present.

Key takeaway: find sensitive data at rest in S3 at scale → Macie (automated discovery plus custom identifiers).

stem: A company runs a real-time multiplayer gaming backend using custom TCP and UDP protocols across multiple AWS Regions. It wants to route players to the optimal regional endpoint based on network performance and automatically fail over if a Region becomes unhealthy, using static IP addresses for firewall allow-listing on the client side. Which service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
Route 53 latency-based routing alone
Amazon CloudFront
An Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS network to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 latency alone: DNS-level, no network acceleration.
• CloudFront: HTTP(S) content delivery.
• ALB: Regional and HTTP only.

Key takeaway: global TCP/UDP acceleration → Global Accelerator.

stem: An application's average API response time has degraded from 200 ms to 1.5 seconds over the past week. CloudWatch metrics show EC2 CPU utilization and Auto Scaling activity for the application tier remain healthy and stable. What should the team investigate next to identify the bottleneck?

choices.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer to cut per-request overhead
Increase the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity
Add CloudFront in front of the API so more requests are served from edge locations
Review RDS Performance Insights for waits, locks, and slow queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With EC2 CPU normal, the slowdown likely comes from the database. Performance Insights shows waits, locks, and top SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB swap: not the bottleneck.
• More instances: EC2 isn't saturated.
• CloudFront: API responses are dynamic.

Key takeaway: find the bottleneck before scaling.

stem: A company operates a self-managed Apache Cassandra cluster on EC2 that requires significant manual tuning and node repair, and still experiences inconsistent read latency under load. To reduce operational overhead while retaining a Cassandra-compatible data model and minimizing application rewrite, which managed service should they consider?

choices.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Neptune
Amazon Keyspaces

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Keyspaces is a managed, Cassandra-compatible service, removing node tuning and repair.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS PostgreSQL: different data model.
• DynamoDB: requires rewriting for a different API.
• Neptune: graph.

Key takeaway: managed Cassandra → Keyspaces.

stem: An API promises 99.9% monthly availability. The SRE team wants to see the remaining error budget in real time and be alerted when the burn rate predicts exhaustion before month-end, with no custom servers. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A monthly Athena query over CloudTrail logs to count failed API calls
Trusted Advisor availability checks reviewed at the end of each month
Route 53 health checks every 30 seconds
Request-based SLOs with burn-rate alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Availability SLOs are best expressed as good requests ÷ total requests. CloudWatch can compute this from ALB metrics (for example, total minus 5xx) with metric math or with Application Signals SLOs, which track error budget and support burn-rate alarms that warn before the budget runs out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: doesn't measure your API's request success rate.
• CloudTrail: records AWS control-plane API calls, not your application's HTTP requests.
• Health check pings: sample availability from outside with coarse probes and miss partial failures that real users experience.

Key takeaway: request-based SLIs, error budgets, and burn-rate alerts are native CloudWatch capabilities.

stem: A company runs a periodic large-scale batch processing job on Amazon EMR and wants to maximize throughput per dollar using a diversified mix of Spot Instance types and Availability Zones, while automatically falling back to On-Demand capacity for core nodes to guarantee cluster stability. Which capability enables this diversified, resilient provisioning strategy?

choices.text: Dedicated Hosts sized for the cluster's peak capacity
A single Spot request for one specific instance type in one AZ
EMR instance fleets with diversified types/AZs and an On-Demand/Spot split
Reserved Instances covering the entire cluster for each run

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR instance fleets let you specify many instance types and AZs, with On-Demand and Spot targets, maximizing Spot availability and throughput per dollar.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive.
• One Spot type in one AZ: interruption-prone.
• RIs for periodic jobs: pays when idle.

Key takeaway: diversified capacity for EMR → instance fleets.

stem: A company implemented a Lambda@Edge function on the CloudFront viewer request event to perform simple, static header manipulation on every request, and now sees higher-than-expected latency and cost at high request volumes. Which change would reduce both latency and cost while preserving the same header-manipulation behavior on every viewer request?

choices.text: Move the function to the origin-request event so it runs only on cache misses
Replace it with a CloudFront Function
Enable provisioned concurrency on the Lambda@Edge function
Increase the memory allocation of the Lambda@Edge function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at edge locations with sub-millisecond startup, which is ideal and cheaper for simple header manipulation on every request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Origin-request: changes behavior; runs only on misses.
• Provisioned concurrency: not available for Lambda@Edge.
• More memory: more cost.

Key takeaway: simple, high-volume edge logic → CloudFront Functions.

stem: A session store runs self-managed Redis on EC2. Manual failover after node failures causes minutes of downtime. The team wants Redis compatibility, automatic failover in seconds, and no patching, and would prefer not to size nodes at all. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: ElastiCache Serverless (Redis OSS or Valkey)
DynamoDB with DAX, rewriting the session code to use DynamoDB APIs
A single-node ElastiCache cluster with daily snapshots for recovery
Self-managed Redis Sentinel on three EC2 instances in different AZs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache Serverless provides a Redis-compatible (Redis OSS or Valkey) endpoint with no nodes to size or patch. Data is replicated across AZs with automatic failover, which removes the manual failover problem. A node-based replication group with Multi-AZ would also work, but requires sizing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed Sentinel: improves failover but keeps patching and operations on the team.
• DynamoDB with DAX: not Redis-compatible, so it requires a rewrite.
• Single node with snapshots: no failover at all, and restores cause downtime and data loss.

Key takeaway: managed Redis compatibility with HA and no node management → ElastiCache Serverless.

stem: A company runs a self-managed PostgreSQL database on an EC2 instance backed by a gp3 EBS volume. During nightly batch reporting jobs, sustained IOPS demand reaches 25,000 while the gp3 volume is provisioned only at the baseline 3,000 IOPS, causing significant query slowdowns; throughput in MB/s is not the limiting factor. What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Increase the gp3 volume size only
Add more EC2 instances behind a load balancer to spread the database I/O
Raise gp3 provisioned IOPS, or move to io2 Block Express
Move the database data files onto Amazon S3 for higher throughput

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sustained I/O above the gp3 provisioned IOPS causes the slowdown. Raise gp3 IOPS (up to 16,000) or move to io2 Block Express for more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Size alone: gp3 performance isn't tied to size.
• More instances: a single database.
• S3 for data files: not how PostgreSQL works.

Key takeaway: gp3 performance is provisioned separately.

stem: An API's average latency is 120 ms and the dashboard looks healthy, yet customers complain. Investigation shows 2% of requests take over 4 seconds. The team wants alerts that reflect customer experience without paging on a single slow request. What should it change?

choices.text: Alarm on the Maximum statistic with one datapoint to catch every slow request
Alarm on p99 with M-of-N datapoints
Alarm on the SampleCount of requests to detect traffic drops
Keep the Average statistic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Averages hide tail latency. A p99 (or p95) statistic shows what the slowest users experience. Requiring M of N datapoints to breach avoids paging on isolated blips while still catching sustained tail degradation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower average threshold: the average stays low when most requests are fast, so the tail problem remains invisible.
• Maximum with one datapoint: pages on any single outlier, causing alert noise.
• SampleCount: measures request volume, not latency.

Key takeaway: alert on percentiles for user experience, and use M-of-N evaluation to control noise.

stem: A critical service must stay fully available with no capacity loss if one Availability Zone fails. It needs 12 instances at peak. The team wants to minimize over-provisioning while meeting this goal. Which deployment fits BEST?

choices.text: Two AZs with 6 instances each (12 total), relying on Auto Scaling to replace capacity
Three AZs with 6 instances each (18 total), so any two AZs still provide 12
One AZ with 12 instances in a spread placement group to avoid shared hardware
Two AZs with 12 instances each (24 total), so either AZ alone covers peak

explanation:
Why this is correct:
To lose no capacity after an AZ failure, the remaining AZs must carry peak load. With N AZs you need peak ÷ (N−1) per AZ. Three AZs give 12 ÷ 2 = 6 per AZ (18 total, 50% extra). Two AZs would need 12 per AZ (24 total, 100% extra), so three AZs meet the goal with less over-provisioning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two AZs with 6 each: after an AZ failure only 6 remain, a capacity loss until Auto Scaling launches replacements, and an AZ event may constrain those launches.
• Two AZs with 12 each: meets the goal but costs more than the three-AZ design.
• One AZ with spread placement: spread placement protects against rack failure, not an AZ outage.

Key takeaway: static stability across AZs means pre-provisioning so the surviving AZs can handle peak. More AZs means less overhead.

stem: A company needs an active-active, multi-Region DynamoDB table where writes made in one Region propagate to replicas in other Regions typically within under a second, with applications in each Region able to read and write locally. Which feature should they use?

choices.text: VPC peering between Regions
DynamoDB Global Tables
DynamoDB Streams feeding a custom Lambda-based replication pipeline
DynamoDB on-demand backup and restore into another Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB Global Tables replicate writes across Regions (typically within a second) in multi-active mode.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering: networking, not replication.
• Custom Streams replication: reinvents Global Tables.
• Backup and restore: not live replication.

Key takeaway: multi-Region active-active DynamoDB → Global Tables.

stem: A company runs a fleet of third-party virtual firewall appliances that all inbound VPC traffic must transparently pass through for inspection, without terminating TLS or altering packet headers, and needs to scale the appliance fleet elastically while distributing flows across appliances. Which AWS load balancing service is purpose-built for this scenario?

choices.text: Classic Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts third-party appliances into the traffic path using GENEVE, with scaling and health checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CLB, ALB, NLB: terminate or route traffic, not transparent inline inspection.

Key takeaway: inline appliances → GWLB.

stem: A company's three-tier application is deployed across three Availability Zones for compute and database tiers, but all outbound internet traffic from private subnets in every AZ routes through a single NAT Gateway located in only one AZ. During a recent outage of that AZ, healthy instances in the other two AZs lost outbound internet connectivity. What change eliminates this single point of failure?

choices.text: Increase the existing NAT gateway's bandwidth allocation
Consolidate all instances into the AZ that hosts the NAT gateway
Replace the NAT gateway with a self-managed NAT instance
One NAT gateway per AZ with AZ-local routes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway in each AZ, with each AZ's private subnets routing to their local one, removes the single-AZ dependency and cross-AZ data charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More bandwidth: still one AZ.
• Consolidate AZs: loses resilience.
• NAT instance: more operations and still single.

Key takeaway: NAT per AZ for resilience.

stem: An existing solution relies solely on nightly AMI snapshots copied to another Region for disaster recovery, yielding an RPO of up to 24 hours. A newly tightened business requirement demands an RPO under 15 minutes for a critical on-premises-replicated workload. Which AWS service should replace the nightly snapshot approach to meet this with continuous block-level replication?

choices.text: AWS Snowball
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication
AWS Backup
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates continuously, cutting RPO from hours to seconds and enabling fast recovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball: offline transfer.
• S3 CRR: objects, not servers.
• AWS Backup: periodic.

Key takeaway: low-RPO server DR → Elastic Disaster Recovery.

stem: Behind an ALB, application processes on some instances hang while the OS stays healthy. The Auto Scaling group uses EC2 status checks only. The team wants hung instances replaced automatically, but not killed during a 5-minute warm-up after launch. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: Set the health check grace period to 0 so failures are detected immediately
Keep EC2 status checks and add a CloudWatch alarm that reboots instances on high CPU
Increase the minimum capacity
ELB health checks with a 5-minute grace period

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With the ELB health check type, the Auto Scaling group replaces instances that fail the load balancer's health check. An application-level path (such as /health) catches hung processes that EC2 status checks can't see. The grace period prevents replacing instances that are still warming up.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU-based reboot: a hung process may not use high CPU, and rebooting doesn't replace the instance through the group.
• Grace period 0: new instances would be marked unhealthy during warm-up and replaced in a loop.
• More minimum capacity: hung instances still receive traffic and return errors.

Key takeaway: the health check must test what actually fails. For application hangs, use ELB or application health checks with an appropriate grace period.

stem: An order service calls a third-party payment API directly and synchronously. During a recent outage of that third-party API, the order service's thread pool became exhausted waiting on timeouts, making the entire order service, including unrelated functionality, unavailable. Which resiliency pattern should be implemented to prevent a single failing downstream dependency from cascading into a full service outage?

choices.text: Retry the failed payment API call indefinitely until the provider recovers
A circuit breaker with bulkhead isolation, plus queue-based decoupling
Increase the timeout for payment API calls so slow responses still complete
Scale the order service out horizontally so more threads are available

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A circuit breaker stops calling the failing provider, bulkheads isolate its resource use, and queue-based decoupling lets orders be accepted and processed later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Infinite retries: exhaust resources.
• Longer timeouts: tie up threads.
• More instances: still wait on the dependency.

Key takeaway: isolate failing dependencies.

stem: A web tier behind an ALB runs in an Auto Scaling group (min 4, desired 6, max 20) with target tracking on request count per target. At 3 AM one instance fails its health check while traffic is low. What does the group do?

choices.text: Waits for a scale-out event
Does nothing until an operator manually replaces the unhealthy instance
Replaces the failed instance to restore 6
Scales in to 4 instances, since low traffic makes the failed instance unnecessary

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-healing keeps the running, healthy instance count at the desired capacity: an unhealthy instance is terminated and replaced regardless of load. Elasticity is separate. Scaling policies change the desired capacity itself in response to load. So the group first restores 6 healthy instances, and target tracking may later adjust the desired count within 4 to 20.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Waiting for scale-out: health replacement doesn't depend on scaling policies.
• Scale in because of the failure: a failure doesn't change desired capacity. Only a scaling policy or schedule does.
• Manual replacement: the whole point of health-based replacement is that it's automatic.

Key takeaway: self-healing keeps desired capacity healthy; elasticity changes desired capacity. They are separate mechanisms that work together.

stem: A company configured Route 53 failover routing with a primary record pointing to an ALB in us-east-1, a secondary record pointing to an ALB in us-west-2, and a health check on the primary. During an outage where the primary application returns HTTP 500 errors while the ALB itself remains reachable and responds to network-level pings, Route 53 does not fail over as expected. What is the most likely misconfiguration?

choices.text: Route 53 does not support automatic failover between records that point to ALBs
Application Load Balancers cannot be targets of Route 53 health checks
The health check tests only TCP reachability, not an HTTP(S) app endpoint
The secondary record's TTL is too low, so resolvers never cache it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A TCP-only health check passes while the application fails. An HTTP(S) check on an application path detects real failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No ALB failover: supported with alias records.
• ALBs can't be checked: they can.
• Low TTL: helps failover, not detection.

Key takeaway: health checks must test what users need.

stem: A company's DynamoDB table uses provisioned capacity with manually set read and write capacity units. During unpredictable viral traffic spikes, the application experiences ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors leading to failed requests, since manual capacity adjustments cannot react fast enough. Which change most directly improves reliability against this single point of failure?

choices.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table to offload reads
Increase the reserved concurrency of the application's Lambda function
Add a global secondary index to spread the read traffic
On-demand mode or auto scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On-demand capacity mode (or auto scaling) adjusts to sudden traffic spikes without manual capacity settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Streams: change capture, not read offloading.
• Lambda concurrency: not DynamoDB capacity.
• GSI: new access pattern, not more capacity.

Key takeaway: spiky DynamoDB traffic → on-demand.

stem: A large enterprise with dozens of business units sharing one AWS Organization wants accurate monthly chargeback reports per business unit, but discovers many resources are inconsistently tagged or missing a required BusinessUnit tag, skewing cost allocation. Which combination of governance controls should they implement to prevent this recurring?

choices.text: A tag policy for BusinessUnit, a required-tags Config rule, and an activated cost allocation tag
Rely on Cost Explorer's untagged-resources filter to find and allocate untagged spend
Audit tags manually each quarter using spreadsheets exported from Resource Groups
Ask each team to tag its own resources and report its spending monthly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A tag policy standardizes the BusinessUnit key, a Config required-tags rule flags untagged resources, and an activated cost allocation tag drives chargeback reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Untagged filter only: finds gaps too late.
• Manual quarterly audits: slow.
• Self-reporting: unreliable.

Key takeaway: enforce tags to make chargeback accurate.

stem: A company runs a web application on an Auto Scaling group with a stable baseline of 10 instances running continuously and occasional bursts up to 30 instances during peak hours. It wants to minimize cost while maintaining reliability. Which purchasing strategy best fits this usage pattern?

choices.text: Reserved Instances for all 30 instances so peak capacity is always discounted
RIs/Savings Plan for the 10-instance baseline; Spot and On-Demand for bursts
Run 100% Spot Instances for the entire fleet to maximize savings
Run 100% On-Demand Instances for the fleet to keep operations simple

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Commit (RIs or Savings Plans) for the steady 10-instance baseline, and use Spot and On-Demand for bursts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RIs for 30: pays for idle peak capacity.
• 100% Spot: risks the baseline.
• 100% On-Demand: overpays.

Key takeaway: commit for the baseline; flexible pricing for bursts.

stem: A cost optimization review flags a db.t3.medium RDS instance as a top contributor to a recent cost spike, due to sustained CPU credit balance depletion and baseline performance throttling that forces nightly batch jobs to run longer, extending billable hours despite the instance appearing 'small.' What does this indicate, and what is the appropriate action?

choices.text: Buy a Reserved Instance for the current db.t3.medium size to lower its hourly cost
It is undersized; move to a non-burstable or larger class, which may cost less overall
The instance is underutilized and should be downsized to db.t3.small
Switch the database instance to Spot pricing during the batch window

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sustained credit exhaustion means the burstable instance is undersized. A non-burstable or larger class may cost less than paying for surplus credits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RI for t3.medium: locks in the wrong size.
• Downsize: makes it worse.
• Spot for RDS: not available.

Key takeaway: burstable instances suit spiky, not sustained, load.

stem: A company serves a globally distributed user base directly from an S3 bucket in a single Region over the internet, and data transfer OUT to the internet costs have grown significantly as usage has expanded internationally. Which architectural change would most directly reduce this transfer cost while also improving performance for global users?

choices.text: Replicate the bucket into every Region where users are located
Put CloudFront in front of the bucket to cache content at the edge
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for all downloads
Move the objects to the S3 One Zone-IA storage class

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content near users, reducing latency and origin data transfer, and its delivery rates are typically lower than S3 direct egress.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicate to every Region: storage cost.
• Transfer Acceleration: adds cost.
• One Zone-IA: storage class, not delivery.

Key takeaway: global delivery → CloudFront.

stem: A company has a very stable, predictable EC2 workload that will remain on the same instance family in the same Region for the next three years, and wants to maximize its discount percentage while accepting reduced flexibility in exchange. Which option typically provides the deepest discount for this scenario?

choices.text: Compute Savings Plans, 3-year term, all upfront
EC2 Instance Savings Plans, 3-year, all upfront
On-Demand Instances with no commitment
Standard Reserved Instances, 1-year, no upfront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For a stable workload on one instance family in one Region, EC2 Instance Savings Plans (3-year, all upfront) give the largest discount.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute Savings Plans: more flexible, smaller discount.
• On-Demand: no discount.
• 1-year no upfront RIs: smaller discount.

Key takeaway: no flexibility needed → maximize discount.

stem: A company is migrating 200 on-premises applications using a mix of AWS Application Migration Service for rehosting, AWS Database Migration Service for databases, and a partner SaaS tool for a subset of custom applications. The migration program office wants a single console to track migration status and progress across all these tools without building custom reporting. Which AWS service should they use?

choices.text: AWS Config
AWS Systems Manager
AWS Migration Hub
AWS Organizations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Migration Hub tracks migration status across tools such as Application Migration Service and DMS in one place.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: resource compliance.
• Systems Manager: operations.
• Organizations: account management.

Key takeaway: migration portfolio tracking → Migration Hub.

stem: A migration factory is sequencing 300 applications into migration waves. Leadership wants early waves to build momentum and refine the migration runbook while minimizing business risk. Which wave prioritization approach best satisfies this goal?

choices.text: Migrate everything in one big-bang cutover to shorten the overall program timeline
Start with low-complexity, low-criticality apps with few dependencies
Migrate the most business-critical applications first to realize ROI immediately
Migrate applications in alphabetical order to keep the process consistent and auditable

explanation:
Why this is correct:
