Early waves should be low-risk, low-complexity apps with few dependencies, building momentum and refining the process.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Big bang: highest risk.
• Most critical first: highest risk while the process is immature.
• Alphabetical: ignores risk and dependencies.

Key takeaway: start simple to build the migration factory.

stem: Discovery data shows that Application A (web tier) has a runtime network dependency on Application B's database, but A and B are owned by different teams and were independently scheduled into different migration waves. What should the migration team do before finalizing the wave plan?

choices.text: Ignore the dependency, since Migration Hub reconfigures application network routes during cutover
Put A and B in the same wave, or keep hybrid connectivity until both move
Migrate B first regardless of A's schedule
Postpone B's migration until every application depending on it has been discovered

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tightly coupled apps should move in the same wave, or keep hybrid connectivity (with acceptable latency) until both have moved.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic reconfiguration: not done by Migration Hub.
• B first regardless: breaks A or adds latency.
• Wait for all discovery: delays unnecessarily.

Key takeaway: plan waves around dependencies.

stem: A company's heavily customized on-premises CRM is expensive to maintain. The migration plan decommissions it, moves its data into a commercial SaaS CRM bought through AWS Marketplace, and rebuilds two critical customizations as integrations using Lambda. Which migration strategy primarily describes the CRM decision?

choices.text: Retire: decommission the CRM with no replacement
Repurchase: replace the application with a SaaS product
Refactor: re-architect the existing CRM as cloud-native services
Replatform: move the CRM to AWS with a managed database

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Repurchase (drop and shop) means moving to a different product, typically SaaS. The existing application is abandoned and its data migrated. Building a few integrations around the new SaaS product doesn't change that the application itself was replaced.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Refactor: re-architects the same application's code. Here the code is thrown away.
• Replatform: keeps the application and makes a few cloud optimizations, such as a managed database.
• Retire: turns off functionality that is no longer needed. Here the CRM function continues in a new product.

Key takeaway: ask what happens to the application. Replaced by a product → repurchase; turned off → retire; code rewritten → refactor.

stem: A legacy .NET application currently runs on Windows Server VMs and connects to a self-managed SQL Server database. The migration team plans to move the application to EC2 largely unchanged, but will switch the database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server to reduce operational overhead, while keeping the application's architecture and code the same. Which migration strategy best describes this approach, and how does it differ from refactoring the same workload?

choices.text: Retiring, because the self-managed SQL Server is being decommissioned as part of the move
Rehosting, because RDS for SQL Server is compatible and the application does not change
Refactoring, because any database migration to a managed service counts as a refactor
Replatforming: same app architecture with one component swapped for a managed service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Replatforming keeps the application architecture but swaps a component for a managed service, such as SQL Server on RDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retire: the app continues.
• Rehost: no component changes.
• Refactor: requires re-architecting code.

Key takeaway: one managed swap, same app → replatform.

stem: Application Discovery Service data collected over a 90-day period shows that an internal reporting application has had less than 2% CPU and network utilization and no active user logins, and the business owner confirms the reports it generates are no longer used. What migration strategy should be applied to this application?

choices.text: Retire the application instead of migrating it
Rehost it as-is to minimize migration risk
Relocate the underlying VMs to VMware Cloud on AWS without change
Repurchase it by replacing it with a SaaS reporting tool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Negligible usage for 90 days suggests the application isn't needed. Retiring it avoids migration and running costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rehost: pays to move something unused.
• Relocate: same.
• Repurchase: buys a replacement for an unused function.

Key takeaway: don't migrate what you don't need.

stem: A company runs several hundred VMware-based virtual machines on-premises and wants to move them to AWS as quickly as possible with minimal changes, while continuing to use existing VMware management tools, vMotion, and licensing during a transition period. Which migration strategy is the best fit, and why is it preferable to a standard rehost using AWS Application Migration Service here?

choices.text: Relocate with VMware Cloud on AWS keeps VMware tooling; MGN rehost converts VMs to native EC2
Refactor, because keeping the VMware tooling requires re-architecting the applications
Relocate and rehost are functionally identical, so either strategy gives the same result
Rehost with MGN, because relocate supports only Windows workloads on VMware

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Relocate with VMware Cloud on AWS keeps VMware tooling and moves VMs quickly without conversion. Rehost with Application Migration Service converts VMs to EC2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Refactor: not needed to keep VMware tooling.
• Identical: they differ in platform.
• Relocate only for Windows: incorrect.

Key takeaway: keep VMware → relocate; go native EC2 → rehost.

stem: Before securing budget approval for a large-scale migration, a CIO needs a data-driven business case comparing current on-premises infrastructure costs against projected AWS costs, based on actual utilization data rather than rough estimates. Which AWS offering is designed specifically to produce this kind of TCO comparison?

choices.text: AWS Cost Explorer forecasts
AWS Migration Evaluator
AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks
AWS Pricing Calculator estimates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Migration Evaluator analyzes on-premises utilization and produces a data-driven business case comparing current costs with projected AWS costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer: analyzes existing AWS spend.
• Trusted Advisor: optimizes existing AWS resources.
• Pricing Calculator: manual estimates without on-premises data.

Key takeaway: migration business cases → Migration Evaluator.

stem: A finance team building a migration business case using AWS Migration Evaluator's QuickInsights report finds the projected savings lower than expected. A deeper review reveals the on-premises TCO baseline excluded data center facility costs, existing software license true-up fees, and staff time spent on patching. What should the team do to produce a more accurate TCO comparison?

choices.text: Assume QuickInsights already includes facilities, licensing, and labor costs and proceed with the case
Use Cost Explorer after the migration to add the missing indirect costs to the business case
Drop Migration Evaluator and rely on Pricing Calculator estimates for the target environment
Run a detailed Migration Evaluator assessment that adds facilities, licensing, and labor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
QuickInsights is a quick view. A detailed assessment adds facilities, licensing, labor, and other on-premises costs, giving a complete comparison.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Assume included: understates on-premises costs.
• Post-migration Cost Explorer: too late for approval.
• Pricing Calculator only: lacks the on-premises side.

Key takeaway: complete TCO needs indirect costs.

stem: A global enterprise configured AWS Migration Hub with its home Region set to us-east-1 and has tracked migrations there for six months. A newly onboarded regional team in Europe configured its AWS Application Migration Service replication and Migration Hub tracking using eu-west-1 as the home Region. The central PMO now cannot see the European team's migration status in the us-east-1 Migration Hub console. What is the cause, and what should be done?

choices.text: Migration Hub synchronizes data across Regions automatically
The European team must delete and recreate their migration jobs in us-east-1 to fix the view
It cannot be resolved; each Region needs a separate Migration Hub with no unified visibility
Migration Hub reports to one home Region; all teams must use the same home Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Migration Hub aggregates tracking data in a single home Region. All teams must use the same home Region to see one consolidated view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic cross-Region sync: not how it works.
• Delete and recreate jobs: unnecessary if configured correctly.
• Unresolvable: choose one home Region.

Key takeaway: one home Region for Migration Hub.

stem: A manufacturing execution system is tightly coupled to plant-floor controllers with millisecond latency needs, and its vendor supports only on-premises installation. The rest of the data center is moving to AWS. The company keeps the system on premises with Direct Connect to AWS and will revisit the decision in 3 years. Which strategy applies to this system?

choices.text: Rehost: lift and shift it to EC2 with Application Migration Service
Retain: keep it on premises for now, with hybrid connectivity
Retire: decommission it and replace it with plant-floor scripts
Relocate: move it to VMware Cloud on AWS unchanged

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retain (revisit) keeps an application in its current environment because of constraints such as hardware coupling, latency, or vendor support, often with hybrid connectivity to migrated workloads and a plan to reassess later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relocate: moves the platform (for example, VMware) to AWS, which is still off premises and conflicts with the controller latency and vendor constraints.
• Rehost: also moves it to AWS, which breaks those same constraints.
• Retire: the system is still needed, so it isn't being decommissioned.

Key takeaway: 'stays where it is for a reason, reassess later' = retain.

stem: A media company needs to migrate 400 TB of files from an on-premises NFS-based NAS to Amazon S3, and wants ongoing incremental synchronization of new and changed files during a multi-week cutover window, with built-in data integrity validation. Which service is the best fit?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
AWS DataSync
AWS Transfer Family
AWS Snowball Edge

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync transfers from NFS to S3 efficiently with incremental syncs, integrity checks, and scheduling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads, not a sync tool.
• Transfer Family: SFTP/FTP endpoints.
• Snowball: offline bulk, not ongoing sync.

Key takeaway: online NFS → S3 with incremental sync → DataSync.

stem: A company needs to migrate 2 PB of archival data from a data center with only a 50 Mbps internet uplink, and the migration must complete within 30 days. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Multiple Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices
AWS Transfer Family with parallel SFTP uploads
S3 Transfer Acceleration over the existing link
AWS DataSync over the existing 50 Mbps link

explanation:
Why this is correct:
At 50 Mbps, 2 PB would take years online. Multiple Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices move data offline within the deadline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Family, Transfer Acceleration, DataSync: all limited by the 50 Mbps uplink.

Key takeaway: do the math on bandwidth; if too slow, ship devices.

stem: A logistics company exchanges shipment manifest files with dozens of external partners over SFTP today, using a self-managed SFTP server on-premises. As part of modernization, they want to retire the self-managed server while keeping the same SFTP endpoints, credential workflow, and partner-facing hostnames, storing incoming files directly in S3. Which service should they migrate to?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect
AWS DataSync
AWS Transfer Family
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoints backed by S3 or EFS, so partners keep using SFTP without a self-managed server.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct Connect: private connectivity, not SFTP.
• DataSync: internal transfers, not partner SFTP.
• Transfer Acceleration: HTTP uploads.

Key takeaway: managed SFTP → Transfer Family.

stem: During a migration, a company's regional offices across three continents report slow upload speeds when copying files directly to a single S3 bucket in us-east-1 over the public internet. The files must land in that specific bucket, and setting up Direct Connect to every office is not feasible in the migration timeframe. What should they enable to improve throughput?

choices.text: A VPC endpoint for S3 in each office's Region
Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in each Region
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
Amazon CloudFront in front of the bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest edge location over the AWS backbone, speeding long-distance uploads to one bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC endpoints: for VPC traffic, not offices.
• CRR: replicates after upload.
• CloudFront: optimized for downloads.

Key takeaway: long-distance uploads to one bucket → Transfer Acceleration.

stem: A company must plan migration waves for 900 VMware VMs. For 50 business-critical servers, it needs running processes and TCP connections between servers to map dependencies; for the rest, inventory and utilization are enough. Guest OS changes on the 850 servers are restricted. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Agentless Collector only, since it also captures process-level network connections
Discovery Agents on all 900 servers so every dependency is captured
A CSV import of server specs into Migration Hub for all 900 servers
Agentless for all VMs, agents on the 50 critical servers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Agentless Collector runs as an appliance in vCenter and gathers VM inventory and performance data without touching guest operating systems, which fits the 850 restricted servers. Discovery Agents installed in the guest OS collect process and network connection data, which is needed for dependency mapping, but only on the 50 servers where they're allowed and valuable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Agents everywhere: violates the guest OS restriction and adds operational effort beyond what's needed.
• Agentless only: doesn't provide process-level connection data for dependency mapping.
• CSV import: static specifications, with no utilization or dependency data.

Key takeaway: agentless = broad inventory and utilization; agent = deep process and network detail. Mix them by server criticality.

stem: A company needs to migrate 150 physical and virtual on-premises servers to AWS with minimal application downtime during cutover, and wants to test the migrated instances in an isolated environment before finalizing the cutover. Which service and approach best satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: AWS Database Migration Service in full-load-only mode for each server's data
AWS DataSync, running a nightly full copy of each server's disks to EBS snapshots
AWS Application Migration Service with block-level replication and test launches
AWS Snowball Edge devices to physically ship server images to AWS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Application Migration Service continuously replicates server volumes at block level, supports test launches, and cuts over with minimal downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS full load: databases only, with downtime.
• DataSync nightly copies: not server migration.
• Snowball: offline and slow for cutover.

Key takeaway: rehost servers → MGN.

stem: A company is migrating a latency-sensitive trading application and needs consistent, high-throughput, low-latency connectivity between its data center and AWS during a multi-month migration, along with a resilient failover path if the primary connection becomes unavailable. Which architecture best meets these requirements?

choices.text: A Site-to-Site VPN connection as the primary path, since it provides more consistent throughput than Direct Connect
Two Site-to-Site VPN connections over different internet providers for both primary and backup, since VPN is just as consistent as Direct Connect
A dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection as the primary path, with a Site-to-Site VPN connection configured as a backup path
AWS PrivateLink configured between the data center and the VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect gives consistent, high-throughput, low-latency connectivity, and a VPN provides backup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPN primary: variable internet performance.
• Two VPNs: still internet-dependent.
• PrivateLink: not data center connectivity.

Key takeaway: consistent hybrid performance → Direct Connect.

stem: A company is migrating a public-facing web application from on-premises to AWS and wants to gradually shift production traffic from the on-premises endpoint to the new AWS endpoint over several weeks, monitoring for issues and adjusting the traffic split as confidence grows, without requiring client-side changes. Which Route 53 routing policy should they use?

choices.text: Latency-based routing, which shifts traffic toward whichever endpoint responds faster
Multivalue answer routing, returning both endpoints' IPs to every client
Geolocation routing, sending selected countries to AWS first
Weighted routing, shifting weight toward the AWS record

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing shifts a growing share of traffic from on-premises to AWS by changing record weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: not controlled shifting.
• Multivalue: no control over proportions.
• Geolocation: country-based, not gradual.

Key takeaway: gradual cutover → weighted routing.

stem: As part of a migration to a multi-account AWS Organizations structure, a company wants its 2,000 employees to sign in once using their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials and access multiple AWS accounts and roles without managing separate IAM users in each account. Which approach should they implement?

choices.text: Configure a separate SAML identity provider trust in each target account manually
IAM Identity Center connected to the existing AD
Amazon Cognito user pools federated independently in each account
IAM users with the same password created in every AWS account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center connects to the existing AD, so employees sign in once and receive permission sets across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• Cognito: for app users.
• Duplicate IAM users: long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO → Identity Center.

stem: A company is migrating an application that requires querying and writing to its existing on-premises Active Directory, for example for group policy and directory-integrated legacy applications, and wants AWS-based servers to authenticate against that same directory without creating a second, separate directory to synchronize. Which AWS Directory Service option should they choose, and why is it preferable to AWS Managed Microsoft AD here?

choices.text: AD Connector and AWS Managed Microsoft AD are functionally identical, so either one works
Simple AD, because it automatically replicates on-premises AD objects into AWS
AD Connector proxies requests to the existing on-premises AD without a new directory
AWS Managed Microsoft AD, because AD Connector cannot serve Windows-integrated applications

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AD Connector proxies authentication and directory requests to the existing on-premises AD without creating a new directory in AWS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: they differ.
• Simple AD replicates on-prem AD: it doesn't.
• AD Connector can't serve Windows auth: it can for supported services.

Key takeaway: use existing AD → AD Connector; need AD in AWS → Managed Microsoft AD.

stem: A company must migrate a 5 TB on-premises Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle with no more than a few minutes of downtime during cutover. Which migration approach best meets this requirement?

choices.text: Export the database, ship it with Snowball Edge, and restore it into RDS during a multi-day outage
Use AWS DataSync to replicate the Oracle data files directly into the RDS instance's storage
Use AWS SCT to convert and copy the data in a single export and import during the cutover window
DMS full load plus CDC, with a brief stop for the final sync

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DMS full load plus CDC keeps RDS in sync while the source stays live. Cutover only requires a brief stop for the final sync.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball export: long downtime.
• DataSync to RDS: can't write RDS data files.
• SCT single export: long downtime.

Key takeaway: minimal downtime → full load + CDC.

stem: A company wants to migrate a commercial Oracle database with extensive PL/SQL stored procedures to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition to reduce licensing costs. Which AWS tool should be used first to convert the database schema and procedural code, before performing the actual data migration?

choices.text: AWS Schema Conversion Tool
AWS Glue
AWS DataSync
AWS Database Migration Service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion) converts Oracle schemas and PL/SQL to PostgreSQL and flags items needing manual changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue: ETL.
• DataSync: files.
• DMS: moves data, not code.

Key takeaway: code and schema conversion → SCT.

stem: A company is consolidating 40 business units, each with its own standalone AWS account created ad hoc over several years, into a governed multi-account structure as part of its migration program. They want standardized guardrails such as preventing root user actions and restricting Regions, a consistent account provisioning process for future accounts, and centralized logging, without building all of this governance tooling themselves. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Migrate all 40 business units into one shared AWS account to simplify governance
Set up a Control Tower landing zone and enroll the existing accounts
Use AWS Config rules in each account without any organizational structure
Apply SCPs manually and independently in each of the 40 accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Control Tower landing zone provides governance, and existing accounts can be enrolled to apply controls consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single account: loses isolation.
• Config without structure: no guardrails.
• Manual SCPs per account: inconsistent.

Key takeaway: govern existing accounts → Control Tower enrollment.

stem: A team is migrating a Java web app in two weeks. It wants AWS to provision the load balancer, Auto Scaling group, and health monitoring, to deploy new versions with zero downtime and quick rollback, and to keep SSH access to instances for troubleshooting. Containers are out of scope. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Lambda with SnapStart and aliases for rollback
Amazon ECS on Fargate with rolling deployments
EC2 instances configured manually
Elastic Beanstalk with immutable deployments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Beanstalk provisions and manages the load balancer, Auto Scaling group, and health reporting for a standard Java app while leaving instances accessible. Immutable deployments, or blue/green using an environment CNAME swap, provide zero-downtime releases and fast rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECS on Fargate: containers are out of scope, and there are no instances to access.
• Lambda: requires re-architecting a traditional web app, which isn't feasible in two weeks and has no server access.
• Manual EC2 with in-place deployments: the team would provision everything itself, and in-place deploys don't give zero downtime or quick rollback.

Key takeaway: fastest managed path for a traditional web app with instance access → Elastic Beanstalk; pick the deployment policy based on the rollback need.

stem: After rehosting an on-premises in-memory analytics application to a general-purpose m6i.2xlarge EC2 instance, the team observes the application frequently swapping to disk and high memory utilization alarms, even though CPU utilization stays low. What is the most appropriate remediation?

choices.text: Move to a burstable T-family instance to reduce cost while memory usage stays constant
Switch to a compute-optimized family such as c6i to increase the memory available per vCPU
Move to a memory-optimized family such as r6i
Enable EC2 Auto Scaling with a target CPU utilization policy to add instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Memory pressure on an in-memory analytics app calls for a memory-optimized family such as r6i.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Burstable T: CPU credits, not memory.
• Compute-optimized: less memory.
• CPU-based scaling: doesn't address memory per instance.

Key takeaway: memory-bound → R family.

stem: A company migrating a set of containerized microservices already has a mature operational investment in Kubernetes: custom Kubernetes operators, Helm charts, and kubectl-based CI/CD pipelines built by the platform team. Which container orchestration service on AWS best preserves this existing tooling and operational model?

choices.text: Amazon ECS, which accepts Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts without changes
AWS Lambda, which can deploy container images directly from existing Helm charts
Amazon EKS, compatible with existing manifests, Helm, and kubectl
AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which natively supports Kubernetes manifests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EKS runs upstream-compatible Kubernetes, so existing manifests, Helm charts, operators, and kubectl workflows carry over.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECS: different API; doesn't accept Kubernetes manifests.
• Lambda: not Kubernetes.
• Beanstalk: not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: keep Kubernetes investment → EKS.

stem: A team migrating a set of containerized batch-processing jobs wants to avoid managing, patching, and scaling EC2 instances for their ECS cluster, and is willing to accept less control over the underlying compute environment in exchange for per-task billing. Which ECS launch type should they choose?

choices.text: AWS Fargate launch type
EC2 launch type using Spot Instances only
EC2 launch type with manual Auto Scaling
ECS Anywhere running on on-premises infrastructure

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs ECS tasks without managing EC2 instances, patching, or cluster scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 with Spot: still manage instances.
• EC2 with manual scaling: more work.
• ECS Anywhere: your own infrastructure.

Key takeaway: no servers to manage for containers → Fargate.

stem: After containerizing, a team needs a private image registry shared by 12 accounts. Images must be scanned for CVEs, tags must not be overwritten, images must be replicated to a second Region for DR, and pulls must stay private from workloads in VPCs without internet access. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: A self-hosted registry on EC2 with a public IP and security groups limited to the accounts
Amazon ECR with its governance and private access features
AWS CodeArtifact repositories shared across accounts, with images stored as generic packages
An S3 bucket storing image tarballs, with a bucket policy for the 12 accounts and CRR for DR

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECR meets every requirement natively: repository policies grant cross-account pulls, tag immutability prevents overwrites, enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector) finds CVEs, registry replication copies images to another Region, and interface endpoints for the ECR API and Docker registry plus an S3 gateway endpoint let private subnets pull images without internet access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeArtifact: a package manager repository (npm, Maven, pip), not a container registry for ECS or EKS image pulls.
• S3 tarballs: runtimes can't pull from S3 directly, and there's no scanning or tag management.
• Self-hosted registry with a public IP: an operational burden, it exposes the registry, and it doesn't serve private subnets without extra networking.

Key takeaway: container images → ECR, and turn on its governance features (immutability, scanning, replication, private endpoints).

stem: A team is migrating a self-managed relational database server to an EC2 instance and needs the data volume to persist independently of the instance lifecycle, support point-in-time snapshots, and be resizable as data grows. Which storage option should back the database's data files?

choices.text: Amazon EFS, which supports the highest IOPS of any storage option for databases
EC2 instance store volumes
Amazon EBS (gp3 or Provisioned IOPS)
Amazon S3, mounted directly as the database data volume through a file gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS volumes persist independently of the instance and provide block storage suited to databases (gp3 or io2 for performance).

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS: network file system, not the best fit for a database's block storage.
• Instance store: ephemeral.
• S3 mounted: not a block device for databases.

Key takeaway: persistent block storage for DBs → EBS.

stem: A company is migrating a Linux-based content management application that runs on multiple EC2 instances behind a load balancer, all of which need concurrent read and write access to the same set of uploaded media files. Which storage service should back this shared file data?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Glacier
Amazon EBS, with a single volume attached to all instances
EC2 instance store volumes replicated across instances
Amazon EFS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS provides a shared POSIX file system that multiple Linux instances can mount across AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glacier: archive.
• Single EBS on all instances: not supported across AZs and needs a cluster file system.
• Instance store: ephemeral and not shared.

Key takeaway: shared Linux files → EFS.

stem: A company is migrating a Windows-based application that relies on an SMB file share integrated with Active Directory for user-level file permissions. Which storage service provides a fully managed, native Windows file share with AD-integrated access control?

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 with IAM bucket policies
AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway
Amazon EFS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares with Active Directory integration and NTFS permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3: object storage, not SMB with AD ACLs.
• Volume Gateway: block storage for on-premises.
• EFS: NFS for Linux.

Key takeaway: Windows SMB + AD → FSx for Windows.

stem: A company wants to migrate its on-premises NetApp-based file storage workloads to AWS while retaining features like NetApp Snapshot technology, SnapMirror replication, and multi-protocol NFS and SMB access from the same volumes. Separately, another workload needs to keep its primary data on-premises but cache frequently accessed data locally while asynchronously storing the full dataset in AWS. Which two services respectively address these needs?

choices.text: Amazon S3 for both cases, using different storage classes
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP for the first case, and AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway for the second
Amazon EFS for the first case, and Amazon FSx for Lustre for the second
AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in cached mode for the first case, and Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP for the second

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for NetApp ONTAP keeps NetApp features such as Snapshots and SnapMirror, and Storage Gateway File Gateway serves the second case of on-premises access to S3-backed storage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 for both: no NetApp features.
• EFS and Lustre: no NetApp features.
• Volume Gateway: block storage, not NetApp.

Key takeaway: keep NetApp features → FSx for ONTAP.

stem: A company is redesigning the data tier for a migrated e-commerce shopping cart service. The access pattern is almost entirely simple key-value lookups and writes by cart ID, traffic is highly variable and spikes 50x during flash sales, and the team wants single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale without manually managing database capacity or sharding. Which database service best fits these requirements?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand or auto scaled)
A self-managed MySQL cluster on EC2 with manual sharding
Amazon RDS for MySQL on a large Multi-AZ instance
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with several read replicas

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Simple key-value access at high scale fits DynamoDB, with on-demand or auto scaling for spiky traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed sharded MySQL: heavy operations.
• Large RDS: relational overhead for key-value access.
• PostgreSQL replicas: read scaling, not key-value scale.

Key takeaway: key-value at scale → DynamoDB.

stem: A company currently self-manages an Elasticsearch cluster on EC2 for full-text search and log analytics, spending significant operational effort on patching, scaling, and cluster management. As part of migration, they want a managed service with a compatible API that reduces this operational burden. Which service should they migrate to?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with full-text search extensions
Amazon DynamoDB with a Global Secondary Index

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch Service is the managed option for Elasticsearch-style search and log analytics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Kinesis Data Analytics: stream processing.
• PostgreSQL full-text search: limited for log analytics.
• DynamoDB GSI: not full-text search.

Key takeaway: managed search and log analytics → OpenSearch.

stem: A company is migrating a legacy application that relies on a specific third-party database engine extension and a custom storage engine plugin that Amazon RDS does not support for that engine. The team must keep this configuration to avoid a costly application rewrite. Which approach should they take for the database tier?

choices.text: Amazon RDS Custom, which allows no customization beyond what standard RDS permits
Self-managed EC2 for full control, accepting more operational responsibility
Aurora Serverless, which automatically supports third-party engine extensions
Standard Amazon RDS with the unsupported extension disabled after migration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A third-party engine extension and custom storage engine need OS and database-level control, which self-managed EC2 provides, at the cost of more operations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS Custom: allows OS access, but the option describes it wrongly as allowing no customization.
• Aurora Serverless: no third-party extensions.
• Standard RDS without the extension: breaks the app.

Key takeaway: unsupported engine customizations → self-managed (or RDS Custom where supported).

stem: A company runs a nightly report-generation job on a dedicated EC2 instance that is idle more than 23 hours a day, executing for only about 10 minutes each night. As part of modernization, they want to eliminate the cost of an always-on instance while keeping the same nightly schedule. Which approach is most cost-effective?

choices.text: Migrate the job to an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of one instance
Keep the instance running but switch to a larger instance type so the job finishes sooner
Buy a Reserved Instance for the job's instance to lower the hourly rate while it runs 24/7
A Lambda function run by EventBridge Scheduler

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A job that runs briefly each night fits a Lambda function triggered by EventBridge Scheduler (if it fits Lambda's limits), paying only for execution time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ASG with minimum one: still idle cost.
• Bigger instance: idle cost remains.
• RI: discounts an idle instance.

Key takeaway: short scheduled jobs → serverless.

stem: After migrating a nightly ETL process to a single AWS Lambda function, the team finds that as data volume grows, the function now regularly fails after hitting its maximum 15-minute execution timeout. The processing logic involves multiple sequential steps, extract, transform, and load, each of which could be retried independently on failure. What is the best modernization approach to resolve this?

choices.text: Increase the function's memory
Rewrite the function in a compiled language so it stays under the timeout as data volume grows
Configure reserved concurrency on the function so it is allowed to run longer than the default limit
Split the ETL into per-step functions orchestrated by Step Functions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Splitting the ETL into steps orchestrated by Step Functions keeps each step within Lambda's 15-minute limit, with retries and state between steps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More memory: helps speed, but volume keeps growing past 15 minutes.
• Compiled language: temporary relief.
• Reserved concurrency: doesn't extend duration.

Key takeaway: work beyond 15 minutes → decompose and orchestrate.

stem: A team is decomposing a monolithic order-processing application into microservices as part of modernization. One service performs long-running, up to 2 hours, CPU-intensive batch reconciliation jobs with variable memory requirements up to 30 GB. Which compute option is most appropriate for this specific service, compared to using AWS Lambda?

choices.text: AWS Lambda, which supports unlimited execution duration for batch workloads
ECS or EKS on Fargate, which allows longer runs and more memory than Lambda
EC2 Spot Instances only, since Fargate does not support long-running tasks
Lambda with provisioned concurrency, which removes the 15-minute timeout

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECS or EKS on Fargate supports long-running tasks with more memory than Lambda, without managing servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited Lambda duration: capped at 15 minutes.
• Spot only: Fargate supports long tasks.
• Provisioned concurrency: doesn't remove the timeout.

Key takeaway: long jobs without servers → containers on Fargate.

stem: A platform team modernizing their deployment pipeline wants to adopt Kubernetes-native GitOps practices, using existing Helm charts and custom resource definitions they have already built for another cloud provider, while offloading management of the Kubernetes control plane to AWS. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Amazon EKS
AWS CodeDeploy
Amazon ECS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EKS supports Kubernetes-native GitOps tools (such as Argo CD or Flux) with existing Helm charts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Beanstalk: not Kubernetes.
• CodeDeploy: not GitOps for Kubernetes.
• ECS: not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: Kubernetes GitOps → EKS.

stem: A legacy application stores user session state and uploaded file attachments on the local disk of each web server, which prevents horizontal scaling because a user's requests must be routed back to the same server. As part of modernization to support Auto Scaling, what should the team do with the uploaded file attachments?

choices.text: Store attachments in S3 via the S3 API instead of local disk
Increase each web server's local disk
Replicate local disks across servers with a nightly synchronization job
Use sticky sessions on the load balancer as a permanent solution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storing attachments in S3 (and sessions in a shared store) removes dependence on any one server's disk, enabling horizontal scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger local disks: still server-bound.
• Nightly sync: stale data.
• Permanent sticky sessions: uneven load and data loss on failure.

Key takeaway: stateless servers scale; move state out.

stem: A team containerizing a legacy application with Amazon ECS on Fargate needs multiple concurrently running Fargate tasks to read and write to the same set of files, since the application was originally designed around a shared local filesystem. Which storage integration should they use?

choices.text: Use EC2 instance store shared via a common AMI
Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each Fargate task
Mount an Amazon EFS file system as a volume in the ECS Fargate task definition
Store the files in Amazon S3 Glacier and mount it directly as a POSIX file system

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate tasks can mount EFS volumes defined in the task definition, providing shared POSIX storage across tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance store via AMI: Fargate has no AMIs.
• EBS per task: not shared among tasks.
• Glacier as POSIX: not possible.

Key takeaway: shared files for Fargate → EFS.

stem: A development team maintains dozens of short-lived test and staging database environments that are used intermittently throughout the day, sometimes idle for hours, and cost control for these non-production databases is a priority. Which Amazon Aurora deployment option best fits this usage pattern, and why?

choices.text: Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity down during idle periods
Aurora with Multi-AZ and two read replicas per environment for maximum availability
Aurora Global Database to replicate each test environment across multiple Regions
A provisioned Aurora cluster on the largest instance class for consistent test performance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity down during idle periods, lowering cost for intermittently used environments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ with replicas: expensive for test.
• Global Database: unnecessary.
• Largest provisioned class: wasteful.

Key takeaway: intermittent databases → Aurora Serverless v2.

stem: A migrated web application's relational database is under heavy read load from repeated queries for the same frequently accessed product catalog data, causing elevated latency during peak hours. As a modernization step to reduce database load without changing the database engine, what should the team introduce?

choices.text: Add another read replica for every 10% increase in traffic
Amazon OpenSearch Service to replace the relational database
AWS Global Accelerator to reduce network latency to the database
Amazon ElastiCache as a cache in front of the database

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache caches frequently read product data in memory, cutting database load and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More replicas per traffic step: costly.
• OpenSearch replacement: different purpose.
• Global Accelerator: network path, not database load.

Key takeaway: repeated reads → cache.

stem: A migrated order-processing application currently has the web front end call the inventory and payment services synchronously within a single request, meaning a slowdown in the payment service directly causes front-end timeouts and lost orders during traffic spikes. As a modernization opportunity, which change would best decouple these components and improve resilience?

choices.text: Scale the front end horizontally while keeping the synchronous calls to downstream services
Move the payment service to a larger EC2 instance type so it processes requests faster
Put an SQS queue between the front end and processing services, with retries and a DLQ
Increase the timeout on the synchronous payment call so slow requests still complete

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A queue decouples the front end from processing: orders are accepted immediately and processed with retries, so slow services don't block users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More front-end instances: still blocked by slow calls.
• Bigger payment instance: doesn't remove coupling.
• Longer timeouts: worse user experience.

Key takeaway: decouple synchronous chains with queues.

stem: A company modernizing its integration architecture needs to route events from dozens of internal microservices and several external SaaS partners to different consumers based on event content and type, using a built-in schema registry to discover and validate event structures, and content-based filtering without writing custom routing logic in each consumer. Which service is best suited as the central event router, compared to using Amazon SNS directly?

choices.text: Amazon SNS, which includes a schema registry and SaaS partner event sources
AWS Step Functions, designed primarily as an event router between SaaS applications
Amazon SQS, which offers the most granular content-based filtering of any messaging service
Amazon EventBridge

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge offers content-based routing rules, a schema registry, and SaaS partner event sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS: no schema registry or SaaS partner sources.
• Step Functions: orchestration, not routing.
• SQS: a queue, not a router.

Key takeaway: event routing across services and SaaS → EventBridge.

stem: An engineer discovers that a production CloudFormation stack shows several resources as MODIFIED after running drift detection, including a security group whose inbound rules were changed manually during an incident. The team wants to reconcile the stack to match the current, drifted production configuration without immediately reverting the manual change, while still being able to manage the resource with CloudFormation going forward. What should they do?

choices.text: Run continue-update-rollback.
Update the template to match the drift, then review a change set before executing.
Ignore the drift, since CloudFormation automatically reconciles drifted resources on the next stack update.
Delete and recreate the stack from the original template so all resources return to their defined state.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the drifted values should be kept, update the template to match them and review a change set before executing; otherwise the next update may revert or fail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• continue-update-rollback: for stuck rollbacks.
• Ignore: CloudFormation doesn't auto-reconcile drift.
• Delete and recreate: disruptive.

Key takeaway: resolve drift deliberately through the template.

stem: A compliance team must deploy the same versioned set of 30 AWS Config rules with remediation to 50 accounts, including accounts added later, and report one compliance score per account for that set. Which AWS Config feature fits BEST?

choices.text: An organization conformance pack deployed from the Config delegated administrator
Individual Config rules created in each account by a StackSet, with scores calculated in a spreadsheet
Firewall Manager security group policies applied across the organization
A Config aggregator in the audit account that pushes the rules to member accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Conformance packs bundle Config rules and remediation actions into one versioned template. Organization conformance packs deploy that bundle to all member accounts, including new ones, and Config reports a compliance score per conformance pack for each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Individual rules via StackSets: they deploy, but the rules aren't managed as a package and there's no native per-pack score.
• Aggregators: collect and display data across accounts. They don't deploy rules.
• Firewall Manager security group policies: manage security groups, not arbitrary compliance rule sets.

Key takeaway: deploy a rule bundle org-wide → organization conformance pack; view results centrally → aggregator.

stem: A Lambda function in Account 111111111111 attempts sts:AssumeRole into a role in Account 222222222222 and receives AccessDenied. The target role's trust policy Principal correctly lists the Lambda execution role's ARN, and the code uses the correct target role ARN. What is the most likely missing piece?

choices.text: The Lambda execution role also needs an Allow for sts:AssumeRole on the target role
STS is a global service and does not support cross-account AssumeRole calls from Lambda
Lambda functions cannot assume roles in other accounts, only roles in their own account
The target role needs a resource-based policy in addition to its trust policy to be assumed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account AssumeRole needs both the target role's trust policy and an Allow for sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN in the caller's (Lambda execution role's) policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• STS doesn't support cross-account: it does.
• Lambda can't assume other accounts' roles: it can.
• Resource-based policy beyond trust: the trust policy is the role's resource policy.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust on the target and permission on the caller.

stem: A Control Tower administrator enables a guardrail that uses an SCP to block disabling CloudTrail in member accounts, and separately enables a guardrail that uses an AWS Config rule to flag accounts where CloudTrail is disabled. How should these two guardrail types be characterized?

choices.text: Both are preventive guardrails
The SCP guardrail is preventive; the Config rule guardrail is detective
The SCP guardrail is detective, and the Config rule guardrail is preventive
Both are detective, because Control Tower supports only detective guardrails

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCP-based guardrails prevent actions. Config rule-based guardrails detect and report noncompliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both preventive: Config rules detect.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Both detective: SCPs are preventive.

Key takeaway: preventive = SCP; detective = Config.

stem: A company has 60 VPCs across 25 accounts, all attached to a Transit Gateway, plus an on-premises data center connected by Direct Connect. On-premises servers must resolve records in private hosted zones owned by several accounts, and VPC workloads must resolve the on-premises domain corp.example.com. Which design has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Run BIND DNS servers on EC2 in every VPC and configure zone transfers from the on-premises servers.
Create inbound and outbound Resolver endpoints in every VPC and replicate forwarding rules manually.
Make all private hosted zones public and restrict who can query them with security groups.
Central Resolver endpoints in a networking VPC with PHZs associated and forwarding rules shared via RAM.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Central Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in a networking VPC, with private hosted zones associated to the VPCs and forwarding rules shared via RAM, give hybrid DNS for all 60 VPCs without per-VPC endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BIND on EC2 everywhere: heavy operations.
• Endpoints in every VPC: costly and duplicated.
• Public zones: expose internal names.

Key takeaway: centralize hybrid DNS; share rules with RAM.

stem: A company centralizes east-west inspection by routing VPC-to-VPC traffic through an inspection VPC attached to a Transit Gateway. The inspection VPC has firewall endpoints in two Availability Zones. Some flows between workloads in different AZs are intermittently dropped by the stateful firewall. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Increase the MTU on the Transit Gateway attachments to 9001 so large flows are not fragmented.
Add a third firewall endpoint in another Availability Zone to spread the stateful load.
Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment.
Replace the Transit Gateway with VPC peering between all VPCs and inspect at each VPC edge.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC's TGW attachment keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ and appliance, preventing asymmetric routing drops by stateful firewalls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU change: unrelated to asymmetry.
• Another AZ endpoint: doesn't fix symmetry.
• Peering everywhere: loses central inspection.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection via TGW → appliance mode.

stem: A company must prevent all accounts in its organization from creating resources outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1. Global services such as IAM, CloudFront, and Route 53 must keep working. Which SCP approach is correct?

choices.text: A Deny SCP with a NotAction list for global services and an aws:RequestedRegion condition.
An SCP that allows only actions in the two Regions, attached to the root in place of FullAWSAccess.
An IAM permissions boundary on every role and user that lists only the two approved Regions.
An SCP that denies ec2:* and s3:* in all Regions other than the two approved Regions.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Deny SCP with a NotAction list exempting global services and a condition on aws:RequestedRegion blocks other Regions without breaking IAM, Organizations, and similar global services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow-only SCP at root: allow lists don't restrict by themselves unless FullAWSAccess is removed, and globals break.
• Permissions boundaries: per principal, easy to miss.
• Deny ec2/s3 only: other services remain.

Key takeaway: Region restriction = Deny + NotAction for globals.

stem: Finance requires that every new EC2 instance and EBS volume in all accounts has a CostCenter tag whose value comes from an approved list. Untagged resources must not be created. Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Activate CostCenter as a cost allocation tag.
An SCP denying creation when aws:RequestTag/CostCenter is missing.
A tag policy defining CostCenter and its allowed values, enforced.
Enable AWS Cost Explorer so untagged resources appear in reports and can be followed up.
Use AWS Config to delete untagged instances automatically after one day.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A tag policy defines CostCenter and allowed values (with enforcement), and an SCP denies creation when aws:RequestTag/CostCenter is missing. Together they enforce presence and valid values.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Activate the tag: reporting only.
• Cost Explorer: reporting only.
• Config auto-delete: destructive and after the fact.

Key takeaway: enforce tags at creation: SCP (presence) + tag policy (values).

stem: A trading platform's connectivity to AWS is business-critical and must survive the failure of a single device, a single connection, or an entire Direct Connect location. Which configuration meets this requirement?

choices.text: One Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as backup.
Two Direct Connect connections at a single location, terminating on separate AWS devices.
One Direct Connect connection using a link aggregation group of two ports on one device.
Separate connections on separate devices at two or more DX locations.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Surviving a device, connection, or location failure requires separate connections on separate devices at two or more Direct Connect locations (the maximum resiliency model).

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX + VPN: VPN has lower bandwidth and different performance.
• Two connections at one location: a location outage takes both down.
• LAG on one device: a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: location-level resilience needs multiple DX locations.

stem: A global e-commerce application uses Aurora MySQL in us-east-1. The business requires an RPO measured in seconds and an RTO under a few minutes if the entire Region fails, and read latency in eu-west-1 must be low. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: An Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in eu-west-1.
A cross-Region read replica using binlog replication, promoted manually during an outage.
AWS Backup with a cross-Region copy rule running every 15 minutes.
Hourly Aurora snapshots copied to eu-west-1 and restored on failure.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates with typical sub-second lag and supports fast managed failover to the secondary Region, meeting seconds of RPO and minutes of RTO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Binlog replica with manual promotion: more lag and slower recovery.
• 15-minute backup copies: RPO of 15 minutes.
• Hourly snapshots: RPO of an hour.

Key takeaway: seconds of RPO for Aurora → Global Database.

stem: A company runs 200 on-premises Windows and Linux servers. It needs disaster recovery on AWS with an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes, while keeping standby compute costs as low as possible. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Use AWS DataSync to copy the servers' file shares to AWS every hour.
Run a full copy of the environment on EC2 in a warm standby configuration.
Back up the servers nightly with AWS Backup and restore them on failure.
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery with a low-cost staging area.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates continuously to a low-cost staging area and launches recovery instances in minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly DataSync: files only, with an hour of RPO.
• Full warm standby: costly.
• Nightly backups: a day of RPO.

Key takeaway: seconds RPO, minutes RTO, low cost → DRS.

stem: A team deploys an Amazon ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer. It wants to run automated tests against the new version on a separate listener before any production traffic shifts, and to roll back instantly if alarms fire after the shift. Which deployment approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: An ECS rolling update with minimumHealthyPercent set to 100 and alarms on the service.
CodeDeploy blue/green with a test listener, validation hooks, and alarm rollback.
Replace the task definition and restart all tasks at the same time after testing locally.
Route 53 weighted records pointing to two separate ALBs, with weights edited manually.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS supports a test listener to validate the replacement task set, lifecycle validation hooks, and alarm-based rollback before production traffic shifts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rolling update: no separate test traffic.
• Restart all at once: no testing or rollback.
• Manual weighted DNS: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: test before shifting → blue/green with a test listener.

stem: Field teams on several continents upload video files of 5-20 GB to a single S3 bucket in us-west-2. Uploads are slow and frequently fail partway through. Which combination BEST improves speed and reliability?

choices.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to buckets on each continent.
Create a CloudFront distribution with the bucket as origin and use GET requests.
Use S3 multipart upload with S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled on the bucket.
Upload through a single large EC2 instance acting as a proxy in us-west-2.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multipart upload makes large uploads resilient (retry parts) and parallel, and Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance transfers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CRR: replicates after upload.
• CloudFront GETs: downloads.
• EC2 proxy: a bottleneck.

Key takeaway: large distant uploads → multipart + acceleration.

stem: An order service publishes events that must be processed in order for each customer, but events for different customers should be processed in parallel. Duplicate processing must be avoided when producers retry. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: An SQS FIFO queue with customer ID as the message group ID, plus deduplication IDs.
An SQS standard queue with a long visibility timeout and idempotent consumers.
An SQS FIFO queue with a single message group ID shared by all messages.
An SNS standard topic with multiple SQS standard queues subscribed to it.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A FIFO queue with the customer ID as the message group ID keeps order per customer while processing different customers in parallel, and deduplication prevents duplicates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard queue: no ordering guarantee.
• Single message group: serializes everything.
• SNS standard: no ordering.

Key takeaway: per-key ordering with parallelism → FIFO message groups.

stem: A Java 21 Lambda function behind API Gateway has p99 latency of 6 seconds caused by cold starts during framework initialization. Traffic is spiky and unpredictable. The team wants to reduce cold-start latency without paying for always-on capacity. What should it do?

choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency equal to peak concurrency.
Move the function into a VPC to reduce network setup time.
Enable Lambda SnapStart on published function versions.
Increase the function timeout to 15 minutes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda SnapStart caches an initialized execution environment snapshot for published versions, cutting Java cold starts dramatically without paying for idle capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned concurrency at peak: works but costly for low traffic.
• VPC attachment: adds, not removes, setup.
• Longer timeout: doesn't reduce latency.

Key takeaway: Java cold starts → SnapStart.

stem: During traffic bursts, thousands of concurrent Lambda invocations open new connections to an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, causing 'too many connections' errors and high CPU on the writer. What is the MOST effective improvement?

choices.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy between Lambda and Aurora.
Add two more Aurora Replicas to spread the incoming connections across more instances.
Lower the Lambda function's reserved concurrency to 1 so only one connection is open.
Increase the writer's instance size.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections, preventing connection storms from bursts of Lambda invocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More replicas: the writer still gets connections.
• Concurrency 1: throttles the application.
• Bigger writer: raises the limit but doesn't pool.

Key takeaway: Lambda + relational DB → RDS Proxy.

stem: A security review finds SSH port 22 open to corporate IP ranges on 400 EC2 instances, with shared key pairs. The company wants to close all inbound ports, remove key pairs, and record every interactive session for audit. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: Rotate the SSH key pairs monthly with Secrets Manager and restrict port 22 further.
Session Manager with IAM access and session logging.
Deploy bastion hosts in each VPC and restrict their security groups to the corporate range.
Use EC2 Instance Connect with port 22 open to the internet and short-lived keys.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Session Manager provides shell access through IAM without open ports or SSH keys, with session logging to S3 or CloudWatch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rotate keys and restrict port 22: still open ports and keys.
• Bastions: still SSH and extra hosts.
• Instance Connect with port 22 open to the internet: exposure.

Key takeaway: close SSH → Session Manager.

stem: A company's bill shows high NAT gateway data processing charges. Analysis shows most traffic from private subnets goes to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region. Which change reduces cost the MOST with minimal effort?

choices.text: Move the workloads to public subnets with public IP addresses.
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance on a larger instance type to avoid processing fees.
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in the private route tables.
Create interface VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in every Availability Zone.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route that traffic privately without NAT processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public subnets: exposure.
• NAT instance: operations, still in the path.
• Interface endpoints: hourly and per-GB costs.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB traffic off the NAT → gateway endpoints.

stem: An application's load rises sharply at 8:00 AM every weekday. Target tracking scaling reacts, but new instances take 7 minutes to become healthy, so users see errors for the first 10 minutes. Which improvement addresses this with the least manual maintenance?

choices.text: Create a scheduled scaling action that must be updated manually whenever the pattern changes.
Enable predictive scaling on the group.
Increase the health check grace period to 15 minutes so new instances are not replaced early.
Lower the target tracking CPU target to 10% so scaling starts as soon as load begins to rise.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling forecasts the recurring 8 AM increase and launches capacity ahead of time, covering the 7-minute startup.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual schedules: need upkeep.
• Longer grace period: doesn't add capacity sooner.
• 10% CPU target: overprovisions all day.

Key takeaway: slow-starting instances + recurring peaks → predictive scaling.

stem: A company is migrating a 4 TB Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Downtime must be under 30 minutes. Which approach meets this requirement?

choices.text: Convert the schema, then DMS full load plus CDC and cut over at near-zero lag.
Use AWS DMS full load only, stopping the application for the duration of the entire load.
Export with Oracle Data Pump, copy the dump to S3, and import into Aurora during a weekend outage.
Use native PostgreSQL logical replication to pull changes directly from the Oracle source.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Convert the schema (SCT or DMS Schema Conversion), then run DMS full load plus CDC and cut over when lag is near zero, keeping downtime within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full load only: downtime for the whole copy.
• Data Pump: Oracle format and long downtime.
• Native PostgreSQL logical replication from Oracle: not possible.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous + short downtime → convert + DMS CDC.

stem: A company must move 80 TB from an on-premises NFS server to Amazon EFS over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link. The source keeps changing until cutover, file permissions and timestamps must be preserved, and data integrity must be verified. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Application Migration Service replicating the NFS server's volumes to EC2.
The aws s3 sync command to an S3 bucket.
AWS DataSync with incremental tasks and a final sync.
AWS Transfer Family, with the NFS data uploaded to EFS over SFTP.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync copies NFS data to EFS over Direct Connect with incremental tasks, and a final sync at cutover captures the last changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MGN: server replication, not NFS to EFS.
• s3 sync: targets S3, not EFS.
• Transfer Family: SFTP, not NFS migration.

Key takeaway: NFS → EFS migration → DataSync.

stem: Before migrating 300 on-premises servers, a company needs process-level information and network dependencies between servers to group applications into migration waves. Which approach provides this data?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks run against the on-premises environment.
Application Discovery Service agents, viewed in Migration Hub.
Importing a spreadsheet of server names and sizes into Migration Hub.
Agentless discovery through the VMware vCenter connector only.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Application Discovery Service agents collect process-level data and network connections, and Migration Hub shows the dependency maps for wave planning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: AWS accounts only.
• Spreadsheet: no dependencies.
• Agentless only: no process-level data.

Key takeaway: dependencies need agent-based discovery.

stem: A company wants to rehost 500 VMware virtual machines to Amazon EC2 with minimal changes, continuous replication until cutover, and the ability to launch test instances without affecting the source. Which service should it use?

choices.text: AWS Database Migration Service with continuous replication.
VM Import/Export for each VM image, scripted in batches.
AWS Application Migration Service (MGN).
AWS DataSync copying VM disks to EBS snapshots.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Application Migration Service replicates VMs continuously until cutover and supports test launches, with minimal changes to the servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DMS: databases.
• VM Import/Export: one-time images without continuous replication.
• DataSync: files.

Key takeaway: rehost at scale → MGN.

stem: A company wants to modernize a monolithic web application into microservices incrementally. Each new service should take over specific URL paths while the monolith continues to serve the rest, with no big-bang cutover. Which pattern and implementation fit BEST?

choices.text: Rewrite the whole application.
Put the monolith behind CloudFront and cache all responses until the rewrite is complete.
Run the monolith and microservices in separate accounts with different URLs for users.
Strangler fig: ALB path rules route selected paths to new ECS services.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The strangler fig pattern routes selected paths (for example, with ALB path rules) to new services while the monolith handles the rest, migrating gradually.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full rewrite: high risk.
• Cache everything: doesn't modernize.
• Separate URLs: breaks the user experience.

Key takeaway: incremental modernization → strangler fig.
